item.title: Use decision models with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations
item.dc:creator: Sungyeon Kim
item.description: Some agent-evaluation questions are narrow and repeatable, and decision models answer exactly that kind of question. This post shows how to connect two decision models, Jev and Strands Decider, to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations through code-based evaluators, and how to validate a decision-model check before you gate a release on it.
item.content:encoded:
Some of the questions you ask when evaluating an agent are narrow and repeatable. Did this response stay on policy? Is this tool call safe to approve? Does this answer match the retrieved context? Decision models answer exactly that kind of question. They take a structured state and a fixed set of allowed answers and return a calibrated probability over them, rather than free-form text whose confidence drifts from run to run. That makes them a strong fit for the scoring step in an agent evaluation, where you want a label and a number you can threshold and trust.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, scores an agent through its entire lifecycle, on demand during development, in batch jobs against stored sessions, and online against production traffic. Alongside 15 built-in evaluators, AgentCore Evaluations supports custom evaluators that you define as either an LLM-as-a-judge or a code-based evaluator. Custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluators apply your instructions and rating scale with a model in Amazon Bedrock. Code-based evaluators run your own logic in an AWS Lambda function, and that logic can call your choice of external system, model, or API, including a decision model.

Decision models suit questions with a fixed set of answers that an informed person could decide at a glance, such as whether the agent refused a request or whether a response stayed on topic. After you validate a question on your own traffic, a decision model can be sufficient for that decision or score, and you can extend the same approach to specific harmfulness or stereotyping categories in your policy. Because both backends can answer several questions about the same state in a single request, you can use them as a screening layer rather than a replacement, running a pass or fail signal across your metrics to select the turns that warrant deeper assessment by the built-in evaluators, whose explanations help you investigate what went wrong.

This post shows how to connect two decision model backends to AgentCore Evaluations through code-based evaluators. The first is Jev, a hosted decision model from TypeSafe. The second is Strands Decider 2B, an open-source decision model you run yourself. By the end of this post, you will know how to convert the AgentCore evaluator input into a decision model request, and the model’s probabilities back into an AgentCore evaluation result. First, though, when should you reach for a custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluator, and when does a decision model fit better? The next section breaks down what a decision model is and the trade-offs involved.

Decision models

A decision model is a small, specialized model trained to select from a fixed set of options and return calibrated confidence scores rather than generating free-form text. A general-purpose large language model (LLM) evaluator produces a score with a rationale. A decision model instead produces a probability distribution over predefined answers. That gives you a direct confidence measure you can threshold, aggregate, and act on programmatically. This makes decision models well-suited for evaluation tasks where the judgment can be stated as a choice among a fixed set of options: “Is this response grounded?” or “Did the agent complete the user’s goal?”

Decision models are most useful when you want a well-calibrated confidence score alongside the label, not just a binary judgment. They are also appropriate when you want to enforce a specific rubric consistently without relying on a general-purpose LLM to interpret it.

Jev, the hosted decision model from TypeSafe, and Strands Decider, an open-source, 2-billion-parameter decision model from the Strands Agents team, both support three types of questions. A noul question poses a yes/no question and returns a probability between 0 (no) and 1 (yes). A choice question asks which of up to 255 options applies, returning the most probable option along with the full distribution and a confidence. A score question asks which of 2 to 10 ordered levels applies, returning a probability-weighted score, the distribution over levels, and a confidence. Many evaluation rubrics fit one of these types. “Is every fact in this response supported by the tool results?” is a yes/no question, and “How helpful was this response, on a four-level rubric?” is a score.

Decision models versus LLM-as-a-judge

The built-in evaluators in AgentCore today use a general-purpose LLM to assess the agent response against a rubric and explain its judgment. This is valuable when the evaluation requires connecting evidence, identifying missing information, or working through a response in depth in tasks where the explanation is as useful as the score. Decision models are not a replacement for LLM evaluators. They’re an addition that the code-based evaluator framework makes possible. Use them for narrow, well-defined checks alongside the built-in evaluators’ broader assessment.

Solution overview

To show how these evaluator types work together, this post builds an end-to-end example of an HR Assistant agent evaluated by deterministic code-based checks, built-in LLM-as-a-judge evaluators, and decision-model evaluators backed by Jev or Strands Decider 2B.

The agent is built with Strands Agents and deployed to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It answers employee questions using five tools that return fixed mock data such as paid time off (PTO) balances, PTO requests, HR policies, benefits, and pay stubs. We use fixed data in this code sample to make it straightforward to verify evaluator behavior from LLM-as-a-judge and decision models. When you additionally have ground truth, you can confirm whether each evaluator catches the right failures. This code sample helps you set up the framework for testing decision models compared to LLM-as-a-judge for your own use cases.

Figure 1: End-to-end architecture of the HR Assistant evaluated by code-based checks, built-in evaluators, and decision-model evaluators backed by Jev or Strands Decider

Prerequisites

To deploy the sample, you need the following:

  • An AWS account in a Region where AgentCore Evaluations is available. The sample defaults to US West (Oregon).
  • Amazon CloudWatch Transaction Search enabled in the account.
  • Access to a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock.
  • Python 3.12 or later, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), and Docker.
  • Jev requires a TypeSafe API key. Visit typesafe.ai for access details.
  • Strands Decider requires a host running the Strands Decider server. You can run it locally for testing, or on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) inside your virtual private cloud (VPC) so the Lambda function can reach it.

Seeing it in action

You can find the full code sample in the AgentCore samples GitHub repository. Two Python scripts handle everything:

  • ../utils/deploy.py deploys the HR Assistant to AgentCore runtime.
  • evaluate.py deploys evaluators, invokes the agent, and runs the evaluation modes.

Running evaluate.py without flags executes five steps:

  1. Creates the Lambda execution role (AgentCoreLambdaEvaluatorRole).
  2. Packages and deploys two deterministic Lambda evaluators: hr-response-length (a trace-level evaluator that checks whether the agent’s response stays within length bounds) and hr-fact-checker (a session-level evaluator that regex-validates HR facts against the known mock data).
  3. Registers both as AgentCore code-based evaluators through the control plane.
  4. Runs on-demand evaluation with EvaluationClient and OnDemandEvaluationDatasetRunner across five labeled scenarios, combining the code-based evaluators with Builtin.Correctness, Builtin.Helpfulness, and Builtin.ResponseRelevance.
  5. Creates an online evaluation configuration that continuously scores live sessions at 100 percent sampling.

At this point you have a working evaluation pipeline with deterministic checks and LLM-as-a-judge scoring. Decision-model evaluators are opt-in. You can add them with a flag, and they run alongside the base evaluators with no changes to the existing flow. Using the flags --with-jev --jev-secret-arn <ARN> deploys jev-evaluator and registers three evaluators: JevGroundedness, JevHelpfulness, and JevGoalCompletion. Using the flag --with-decider deploys strands-decider-evaluator and registers the same three evaluators backed by Strands Decider 2B. Add --decider-ec2 to auto-provision the Amazon EC2 instance, security groups, IAM role, and Lambda VPC configuration without manual console steps.

Figure 2: The evaluation pipeline deployed by evaluate.py, from deterministic checks through built-in and decision-model evaluators

Each decision-model backend contributes three evaluators:

Evaluator Level Question type Label Value
JevGroundedness / DeciderGroundedness TRACE noul Grounded or Ungrounded P(grounded)
JevHelpfulness / DeciderHelpfulness TRACE score (4-level) Most probable level Expected level, scaled 0–1
JevGoalCompletion / DeciderGoalCompletion SESSION choice (3-way) Most probable option Probability-weighted value

Build the evaluator with decision models

Using the flags --with-jev and --with-decider creates a custom code-based evaluator, where you have complete control of the code you want to run as your evaluator. We create AWS Lambda functions where the decision model is invoked inside an AWS Lambda function and returns a label or a numeric value. This Lambda function is registered as the code-based evaluator in AgentCore Evaluations.

The Lambda that is registered as the evaluator receives OpenTelemetry spans of the agent. The spans.py module normalizes the shapes OpenTelemetry content can arrive in and then formats it appropriately to make the call to the decision model. For trace-level evaluation, only the targeted turn and brief prior history are sent, whereas the full conversation is included for session-level.

Figure 3: How the code-based evaluator Lambda adapts OpenTelemetry spans for the decision model and maps the result back to AgentCore

The adapter converts the model’s probability distribution into a result that AgentCore evaluation expects. For a noul question, the probability of true becomes the value and the most probable answer becomes the label. For a score question, the value is the probability-weighted expected level scaled to [0, 1]. For a choice question, it is the weighted average of predefined option values.

Validate a decision-model evaluator on your own traffic

When you rewrite a rubric as a decision model question, you’ve created a new measurement rather than a copy of the old one. A reframed rubric often lands stricter or looser than the original intended, and you won’t see that drift until you check it against real sessions. Before you gate a release on a decision-model evaluator, validate it the same way you’d validate any new measurement, against a labeled sample of your own traffic. The goal of this section is to walk you through that validation end to end, so you finish with an evaluator you can threshold with confidence.

The procedure has five steps.

Step 1. Build a labeled sample. Pull a set of stored sessions from your agent’s traffic, with enough coverage of the failures and edge cases you care about. A sample that covers only the happy path tells you nothing about where the evaluator breaks.

Step 2. Get human reference labels. Have three independent labelers score each turn for the property your question measures and take the majority vote as the reference label. Keep track of which turns were unanimous and which were split. Although unanimous turns are the clear-cut cases, the split-vote turns are the valuable ones, because they reveal ambiguity in the rubric itself before the model ever sees it.

Step 3. Run both evaluators on the same inputs. Run the decision-model evaluator and the matching built-in evaluator over those same sessions in a single batch evaluation. Scoring identical inputs is what makes the comparison apples to apples.

Step 4. Read the results through three lenses. With the majority-vote labels and the easy and hard split in hand, you can now answer the three questions that tell you whether the evaluator is ready.

  • Agreement rate: does it match your humans? Measure how often each evaluator agrees with the majority-vote labels, and do it per question, since one question’s accuracy says nothing about another’s. Then break the numbers out by easy (unanimous) and hard (split-vote) cases. An evaluator that stumbles only on the hard cases is behaving a lot like your human labelers did, which is exactly what you want.
  • Calibration: do the confidence scores mean something? Group turns by the evaluator’s reported probability and compare each group’s agreement with the labels. Higher confidence should track higher accuracy. Then check whether easy cases consistently draw higher confidence than hard ones. If they do, the model’s uncertainty is tracking genuine ambiguity, and you can use those groups to pick a decision threshold per evaluator instead of defaulting to 0.5.
  • Disagreement analysis: where and why do they differ? Find the turns where the two evaluators disagree with each other, and check whether those are the same turns your humans found ambiguous. Read them. Most disagreements trace back to the wording of the question, and a revised question clears them up. When the errors cluster in the hard cases, the rubric is the problem rather than the model.

Step 5. Re-run the check when anything changes. Treat this as a repeatable check rather than a one-time gate. Any time you reword a question or move to a new model version, run it again. Each result’s explanation records the model version that produced it, so you know which version a given score came from.

Choosing the best set of evaluators for your agent

The built-in evaluators remain the foundation of broad evaluation strategy in AgentCore Evaluations. They assess the response against a rubric and its supporting context, and explain the judgment so developers can investigate what went wrong. For the HR Assistant, a faithfulness evaluation can identify a claim that contradicts a tool result, whereas a helpfulness evaluation can point out that the agent answered a balance question but left a requested action incomplete.

Faithfulness, helpfulness, and correctness can require connecting evidence, identifying missing information, or working through a solution. The preprint JEV-as-a-Judge: Accept When Confident, Escalate When Unsure describes a related distinction as “reading versus deriving.” A narrow decision-model check can flag a turn for attention, whereas the built-in evaluator provides the broader assessment and reasoning needed to review it. Decision models shine brightest when you treat them as a gate rather than a replacement. The cascade pattern works like this. First, run a fast, calibrated decision model on every turn of every session to get a cheap pass/fail signal. Then invoke a full LLM evaluator only on sessions where the signal falls below your threshold.

Figure 4: The cascade pattern, where a calibrated decision model screens every turn and only low-confidence turns escalate to a built-in evaluator

Criterion LLM as Judge Decision Models as Judge
Output Score + explanation Calibrated probability
Latency 2–10 s ~hundreds of ms (network)
Customizable Limited (fixed prompt templates) Question definitions
Best for Qualitative nuance, explanation Calibrated judgment

We recommend the following setup:

  1. Configure online evaluation with the built-in evaluators you rely on, as the standard measure of quality across your agents.
  2. Add decision-model evaluators for domain-specific yes/no and choice questions to the same configuration, along with deterministic code-based evaluators for anything you can compute exactly.
  3. Each week, or on whatever schedule suits your release cycle, query the online results for sessions where a decision-model check failed or scored near its threshold, and run batch evaluations on those sessions with the built-in evaluators to get explanations.
  4. Gate releases on the built-in evaluators and on the decision-model evaluators you have validated against labeled data, and track how often the two agree.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, run the cleanup.py that deletes the agent hosted on AgentCore runtime, the evaluators and evaluation config, the AWS Lambda functions that are registered as the evaluators, the EC2 instance that hosts the Strands Decider model, AWS Secrets Manager key and the associated log group on CloudWatch.

Conclusion

In this post, you connected two decision models, Jev and Strands Decider, to AgentCore Evaluations using code-based evaluators, and the accompanying code sample gives you a framework for testing those models and seeing where they add value as evaluators. The built-in evaluators remain your baseline. Decision models add narrow, validated checks that come with a measure of certainty you can threshold and act on. The practical path forward is to add decision-model checks alongside the built-in evaluators you already run, measure how often they agree with your reference labels on your own traffic, and expand coverage only once you trust them.

To get started, review the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations documentation, integrate custom evaluators using code-based evaluators and take a deeper look into Strands Decider model. Get started with code samples by deploying the sample evaluators from the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore sample repository.

item.title: Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick: Human oversight where it matters
item.dc:creator: Steve Vinsik
item.description: Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick reviews eligible agent actions within your existing controls, reducing unnecessary approval prompts while keeping consequential decisions with a person. See how policy sets the boundary, how a classifier reviews actions, and how AWS CloudTrail and Amazon CloudWatch Logs support audit.
item.content:encoded:
How should security leaders preserve human oversight as AI agents take on more work? Permissions establish which actions agents can take, but a permitted action can still warrant a person’s judgment. Requiring approval for every step might seem like the safest approach, yet multi-step tasks can produce repeated prompts, even for routine actions. Research on security warnings shows that attention and adherence can decline with repetition. The challenge isn’t to require more approvals, but to preserve attention for decisions that need human review.

Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick addresses this challenge by reviewing eligible actions within your existing controls. It evaluates each proposed action against the user’s request and either approves it automatically or returns it to the user for review. It does this without granting additional permissions or removing required human approvals. Security leaders retain control over which actions must always go to a person, while Smart Approvals is designed to reduce unnecessary interruptions in routine work.

Figure 1: Policy determines eligibility. Smart Approvals approves eligible actions or returns them to the user for review. Policy denials remain blocked

Policy sets the boundary

Quick evaluates each proposed action against Custom Permissions, Quick Guardrails, connector action permissions, and the user’s settings before automated review. Denied actions remain denied, and mandatory human approvals still apply. With Smart Approvals enabled, an action is eligible only when the user’s setting is “Ask each time” and no other control requires human approval. Connector action permissions, configured when a connector is created, can require human approval for specific actions.

Administrators use Custom Permissions to determine who can use Smart Approvals. It’s on by default, but profiles with deny-by-default enabled must explicitly allow it. Users can also turn Smart Approvals off for themselves. That choice applies across conversations and scheduled runs. When it’s off, actions otherwise eligible for automated review require the user’s approval, and no account-level setting can turn it back on for them.

How eligible actions are reviewed

Smart Approvals uses a separate model, the classifier, to evaluate eligible actions against the user’s request and a bounded view of the conversation. It considers what the action does, where data goes, and who it affects. It can consult the user’s knowledge graph, which contains people and working relationships drawn from connected sources. This helps it understand how recipients relate to the user, such as whether a recipient is in the user’s reporting chain. This lookup stays within your Quick account. Quick doesn’t use the content the classifier reviews, including knowledge graph data, to train models or improve the service.

An action can match the request and still warrant human review. Examples include sending content outside the organization or to senior leaders in the user’s reporting chain, changing access, deleting records, or initiating payments. This list isn’t complete, and the classifier also weighs the surrounding context. Reviewing actions against the user’s request adds a check against indirect prompt injection, where instructions in retrieved content attempt to redirect the agent. Quick instructs both the agent and classifier to treat that content as information, not instructions. Model review can still make mistakes, so actions that must always receive human approval, including those that move sensitive data, should require it through connector action permissions.

The classifier provides judgment. The permission service enforces authority. Each automatic approval is single-use, applies only to the exact action and parameters reviewed, and grants no ongoing permission. Quick labels automatic approvals in the conversation. Actions the classifier doesn’t approve return to the user, as do timeouts and other review failures, which never grant automatic approval. These enforcement boundaries limit what an approval authorizes. They don’t establish that the classifier’s judgment was correct.

When an action goes beyond the request

An account manager asks Quick to prepare a quarterly business review brief for AnyCompany using her team’s account notes and last quarter’s email. She then asks Quick to send it to two colleagues she names. Assuming the send is eligible for automated review, Smart Approvals evaluates the proposed action against her request and the available conversation context.

Now suppose an account note says the brief should also go to an all-sales distribution list of about 2,000 people. That would change the audience beyond the recipients she specified, so Smart Approvals is designed to return the proposed send to her for review, where she can decline it. An approval to send to the original recipients can’t be reused for the wider audience.

Audit evidence and investigation

The Quick permission service records permission updates associated with Smart Approvals in AWS CloudTrail in your account. Each event identifies the user, connector, action, and time, and marks the request as associated with Smart Approvals. That marker doesn’t establish that the permission service accepted the grant or that the action ran. Quick also records permission-check verdicts, including denials from connector action permissions, and changes to a user’s Smart Approvals setting.

Investigators can correlate these events by user and time with other Quick activity in CloudTrail and logs delivered through Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Chat logs capture the user’s request, system response, and conversation context. Agent metadata logs record changes to agents. Records from the destination system, such as a sent email or updated ticket, confirm whether the action completed. Together, these sources help reconstruct what happened without treating approval as proof of execution. CloudTrail Event history retains events for 90 days, so configure a trail for longer investigations. Because chat logs can contain sensitive content, restrict access and consider CloudWatch Logs data protection policies to mask sensitive data.

Where to start

Because Smart Approvals is on by default, begin by confirming that actions requiring human approval are configured through connector action permissions. Set up a CloudTrail trail and delivery of chat logs and agent metadata logs to CloudWatch Logs to support investigations. Chat logs capture only activity after delivery is configured, so earlier approvals will lack that conversation context. With approval requirements and logging in place, use Custom Permissions to limit Smart Approvals to a pilot team working on a defined workflow before extending it to other teams.

Before the pilot, define what success looks like: fewer prompts for routine actions, with consequential actions still returning to a person for review. During the pilot, review a sample of automatic approvals and test high-impact cases, such as sending content outside the organization or adding a recipient introduced by a document. Confirm that these cases come back to the user. Confirm that your team can trace each action from approval through execution. Expand to more teams and workflows only when the results meet those criteria, and reassess as actions and policies change.

The measure of effective oversight isn’t how often an agent asks for approval, but whether people retain control over consequential decisions. For security leaders, the case for expanding Smart Approvals should rest on evidence from the pilot. Fewer prompts are valuable when they preserve attention without weakening accountability.

For setup steps, see Smart Approvals in the governance section of the Amazon Quick User Guide.

 

About the author

Steve Vinsik

Steve is a Principal Product Manager at AWS, where he leads governance, identity, and security for Amazon Quick. He works directly with enterprise CIOs and CISOs to define the controls their organizations need to adopt AI agents at scale, such as access permissions, guardrails, model management, data loss prevention, and observability. Before joining Quick, Steve led product for AWS Identity, including AWS IAM Identity Center and AWS Builder ID, which he scaled from launch to millions of users. He has more than 25 years of experience delivering mission-critical security programs for government customers, with executive roles at General Dynamics, Unisys, and Safran.

item.title: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code
item.dc:creator: Yoonseo Kim
item.description: In production AI agents, context management is the real bottleneck. This post presents a four-layer context engineering framework (architecture, prompts, file-based tools, and verification agents), implemented in working code from Deep Insight, an open source multi-agent data analysis solution on the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
item.content:encoded:
When production AI agents handle tasks such as data analysis and report generation, context management can become a major bottleneck. A 200K-token window sounds generous until a real-world task burns through most of it in minutes. Data analysis and report generation leave the agent failing mid-execution, losing accuracy, or driving up costs. A body of published guidance already addresses this, but the individual techniques are easier to read about than to apply. Applied together, they make a measurable difference: in the reference implementation this post walks through, a single write-and-execute tool cuts the tokens each script adds to context by about 95 percent, and loading skills on demand shrinks the system prompt by about 97 percent.

This series organizes that guidance into practices you can apply directly. Anthropic’s engineering posts, together with features built into the Strands Agents SDK, converge on four layers of context engineering: isolate context at the architecture level, control it through prompts, externalize it to the filesystem, and verify it with independent agents and safeguards. In this post (Part 2), you will learn how each layer works and what it looks like in working code. We applied these techniques in Deep Insight, an open source multi-agent data analysis solution built on the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which serves as the reference implementation throughout.

Post series

  • Part 1: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them.
  • Part 2: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code.
  • Part 3: Harness engineering in practice: moving Deep Insight from dev to production. (Coming soon!)

The first post defined five core challenges that production multi-agent systems must solve. It introduced how Strands Agents SDK, Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore, and AWS Fargate each address different layers of the problem, with code examples. This second post takes the four layers of context engineering practice that sit on top of that architecture and shows each one implemented. The third post guides you through deploying and operating agents in a secure private network on Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), covering everything needed for real-world operations.

What is context engineering?

Context engineering is the discipline of optimizing the information in a large language model (LLM)’s limited context window so agents perform at their best. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5, available on Amazon Bedrock, offers a 200K context window, but complex production tasks quickly exceed it. For example, a seemingly straightforward request like “Analyze sales data and create a DOCX report” runs through several stages: data loading and exploration (5 min), category-based sales analysis (3 min), generating five charts for time-series analysis (10 min), statistical validation (3 min), and final report generation (5 min). Together they consume over 150K tokens across 15 minutes.

Processing such tasks in a single context causes problems: the window overflows mid-task, stale context degrades performance, and errors require re-running the whole pipeline. As context grows, attention to important information drops, and inefficiency raises cost under per-token pricing.

“As the number of tokens in the context window increases, the model’s ability to accurately recall information from that context decreases (Context rot).”

— Anthropic, “Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents” (2025.09)

Context engineering solves exactly these problems, and it is not only a collection of techniques. Spanning architecture design, prompt writing, tool implementation, and verification, it’s a layered discipline where each layer compensates for what the previous ones miss. This post details the four-layer approach you can apply to manage context efficiently.

How to handle tasks that exceed the context window

Anthropic has published several techniques for handling long-horizon tasks. Deep Insight groups these techniques into four layers, with each layer addressing the limitations of the others. The following table sets out the four layers.

Layer Practice Core Principle Limitations
Layer 1: Architecture Isolating Context Through Multi-Agent Architecture Each agent operates in an independent context When isolation alone is not enough
Layer 2: Prompt Output Control and Behavioral Rules Limiting context intake through prompts When prompts alone are not enough
Layer 3: Tools File-based Context Externalization Keeping heavy content in files outside the context When issues still arise
Layer 4: Verification Agents and Safeguards Independent Verification and Safeguards Catching errors and preventing context overflow Final line of defense

The sections that follow take each layer in order, stating what the layer prescribes, why the preceding layers alone are insufficient, and how the practice is implemented in Deep Insight.

1. Isolating context through multi-agent architecture

Give each specialized agent its own context window and pass only compressed results to the orchestrator. Deep Insight does this with a hierarchy of Coordinator, Planner, Plan Reviewer, Supervisor, and Tool Agents (Coder, Validator, Reporter, Tracker, Auditor).

With a single agent, all information, from user requests through data exploration, analysis, chart generation, validation, and reporting, accumulates in one context and easily exceeds the window. Giving each agent its own context keeps even the Coder, which uses the most, under 25K tokens total. Each agent receives only what it needs and signals others with a completion notice and brief summary.

The key to isolation is minimizing shared information. Deep Insight uses a Python dictionary, shared_state, that stores only four things:

  • messages: The previous agent’s final message (not the full conversation history).
  • clues: Compressed summaries collected from each agent.
  • full_plan: A checklist generated by Planner and updated by Tracker.
  • history: A brief log of agent names and messages.

The clues use a fixed CLUES_FORMAT: instead of each agent’s full conversation (tens of thousands of tokens), only compressed core results are passed.

# coder_agent_tool.py -- context passing format
CLUES_FORMAT = "Here is clues from {}:\n\n<clues>\n{}\n</clues>\n\n"
RESPONSE_FORMAT = "Response from {}:\n\n<response>\n{}\n</response>\n\n*Please execute the next step.*"

# After Coder completes: add only compressed result to clues
clues += CLUES_FORMAT.format("coder", response["text"])

This pattern is the one recommended in Anthropic’s “How We Built Our Multi-Agent Research System” post, which describes an orchestrator-worker pattern in which a lead agent delegates to specialized subagents, with each agent working only within its own context. You do not need to build it yourself: the agents-as-tools pattern in the Strands Agents SDK provides this isolation at the framework level.

2. Controlling context inflow through prompts

Layer 1 isolation alone is not sufficient: even with independent contexts, an agent that generates long responses inflates the Supervisor’s context. Layer 2 limits each agent’s output through prompts.

For Deep Insight, we use prompts to limit how much information each agent returns to the Supervisor. Three rules do most of the work, as Deep Insight’s prompts show.

“Start with the strongest model and a simple prompt. Then incrementally add specific instructions based on actually observed failure cases.”

— Anthropic, “Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents” (2025.09)

Implementation detail 2-1: Explicit per-agent output token budgets

Each agent’s prompt specifies a maximum response token count, preventing long responses that pollute the Supervisor’s context.

Agent Output Token Budget Reason
Coder 1,000–1,500 tokens Analysis code is saved to files, so the agent returns only a summary of state, completed tasks, and insights
Validator 800 tokens Validation results are saved to citations.json. The agent returns only a summary
Reporter 1,000 tokens The agent generates the report as a DOCX file and returns only a summary of the result

Anthropic’s ” Writing Effective Tools for Agents” post suggests giving tools a CONCISE or DETAILED response option for context efficiency. Apply the same idea one level up, in each agent’s system prompt. In Deep Insight, all agents share one standardized format:

## Status
[SUCCESS | PARTIAL_SUCCESS | ERROR]
## Completed Tasks
- [Task 1 from FULL_PLAN -- use exact wording so Tracker can match]
- [Task 2 -- be specific, not generic]
## Key Insights
- [Key finding 1 with numbers and ratios]
- [Key finding 2 with business implications]
## Generated Files
- ./artifacts/chart.png -- brief description
- ./artifacts/calculation_metadata.json -- N calculations

Implementation detail 2-2: Self-contained code philosophy

The Coder agent’s prompt explicitly states “variables do not persist between scripts.” Every script must include all necessary imports and load data directly. The prompt provides both incorrect and correct examples:

# WRONG -- Attempting to use a variable from Turn 1 in Turn 2
# Turn 1:
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')
total = df['Amount'].sum()

# Turn 2:
print(f"Total: {total}")  # NameError: name 'total' is not defined

# CORRECT -- Every script is self-contained
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('./artifacts/cache/df_main.csv')  # Load from cache
total = df['Amount'].sum()
print(f"Total: {total}")

The reason this rule relates to context engineering is that referencing variables from previous scripts requires the agent to “remember” prior conversations, which means past code must remain in context. The self-contained principle means past code can be safely removed from context.

Implementation detail 2-3: Supervisor’s section completion rule

The Supervisor’s prompt includes the rule “Do not move to the next agent until all checklist items in the current agent’s section are marked [x].” We express this rule in the prompt because deciding whether the Coder’s work is complete requires the Supervisor to interpret the plan using information from the Tracker’s updates. This judgment is difficult to express in code alone.

3. “Only pointers in context, actual data in files”

Layer 1 isolates context between agents, and Layer 2 limits output within agents. But when the Coder agent generates 100 lines of Python code, that code itself enters the context. Even with “respond briefly” prompt instructions, some code can’t be written briefly. Layer 3 uses tool design to move heavy content outside the context, into the filesystem. Four techniques carry most of the benefit, as the following implementation details show.

Implementation detail 3-1: Moving code outside context with Write and Execute Tool

The Coder reads the analysis plan, writes Python, and executes it to generate visualizations. But when the code gets long, the conventional approach (separate file-write and execute tools) adds 100 lines directly to context per script, accumulating over 1,000 lines.

The fix is to collapse the two steps into a single tool, so the code never enters context as a message. Deep Insight’s Coder agent uses one write_and_execute_tool for this.

Here’s part of the write_and_execute_tool. After writing and executing the file, it returns only a summary: “Wrote 105 lines, execution successful, completed analysis of five categories.” The code stays in the file and about three lines of summary remain in context. Based on this example, that saves about 95 percent of the tokens.

# write_and_execute_tool.py
def _handle_write_and_execute_tool(file_path, content, timeout=300):
    """Write a Python script and immediately execute it."""
    # Step 1: Write file
    with open(file_path, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        f.write(content)
    # Step 2: Execute immediately
    result = subprocess.run(
        f"python {file_path}",
        shell=True,
        capture_output=True,
        timeout=timeout
    )
    # Return only summary
    return f"Written {len(content.split(chr(10)))} lines to {file_path}\n" \
        f"Execution successful\n" \
        f"Output: {result.stdout[:500]}"  # Only first 500 chars

“Server-side filtering: filtering data at the execution layer before it reaches context, 98.7% token reduction (150K to 2K).”

— Anthropic, “Code Execution with MCP” (2025.11)

Implementation detail 3-2: Reusing common logic as modules in the Coder agent

Common modules get reused across analyses. Rather than regenerating them each time, define frequently-used functions as a module once and import them, which prevents token waste and context duplication.

Without this, defining functions like to_python_type() or track_calculation() in every analysis produces 200–300 lines of duplicate code across 10 analyses. Deep Insight generates a module called coder_analysis_utils.py before the first task. It includes functions for converting numpy types, tracking calculation metadata, and saving to JSON. Subsequent analyses import it, replacing 20–30 regenerated lines with two import lines, which saves tokens and improves consistency and debugging.

# coder_analysis_utils.py -- common module generated before first task
import numpy as np
import json
from datetime import datetime

_calculations = []

def to_python_type(value):
    """Convert numpy/pandas types to Python native types"""
    if isinstance(value, (np.integer, np.int64)): return int(value)
    elif isinstance(value, (np.floating, np.float64)): return float(value)
    elif isinstance(value, np.ndarray): return value.tolist()
    return value

def track_calculation(calc_id, value, description, formula,
                      source_file, source_columns, importance):
    """Track calculation metadata -- Validator independently verifies later"""
    _calculations.append({
        "id": calc_id, "value": to_python_type(value),
        "description": description, "formula": formula,
        "source_file": source_file, "source_columns": source_columns,
        "importance": importance
    })

def save_calculation_metadata(path="./artifacts/calculation_metadata.json"):
    """Save all tracked calculations to JSON"""
    with open(path, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        json.dump({"generated_at": datetime.now().isoformat(),
                   "calculations": _calculations}, f, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)

Implementation detail 3-3: Saving and sharing analysis results through structured note-taking

We use structured note-taking to share detailed analysis results without passing them through each agent’s context. Deep Insight stores these results in a file called all_results.txt, which is then read by agents as needed.

For example, the Coder agent appends results to all_results.txt after each analysis task:

with open('./artifacts/all_results.txt', 'a', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write(f"""
## Category Sales Analysis (completed at: 14:32)
- Top revenue category: Fruit (417,166,008 KRW, 45% of total)
- Top 3 categories: Fruit, Vegetables, Meat (78% of total)
- Generated file: ./artifacts/category_sales_chart.png
""")

The Coder records detailed results in this file after each analysis, and the Reporter reads it when writing the final report. Other agents collaborate through all_results.txt the same way.

Without note-taking, the Coder passes detailed results to the Supervisor after every task, accumulating in its context. With note-taking, only an approximately 30-token message like “Category sales analysis complete, 3 key insights found, detailed results saved to all_results.txt” is passed, and the Reporter reads the file when needed.

The pattern generalizes beyond a single file. The filesystem itself can serve as the inter-agent communication bus, as it does in Deep Insight:

File name Producer Consumer Role
all_results.txt Coder Reporter Cumulative log of analysis results
calculation_metadata.json Coder Validator Record of numeric calculations: sources, formulas, and values (for verification)
citations.json Validator Reporter Verified citation data (inserted as [1], [2] in the report)
audit_findings.json Auditor Reporter Citation defects found in the final report (drives targeted Reporter retries)
coder_analysis_utils.py Coder All scripts Shared utility functions (write once, import repeatedly)
full_plan (shared_state) Planner/Tracker Supervisor Checklist status (updating [x])

“The”just in time” approach, dynamically loading data into context at runtime rather than pre-processing all relevant data up front, keeps context fresh, relevant, and adaptive to the evolving state of the task.”

— Anthropic, “Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents” (2025.09)

Implementation detail 3-4: Loading only needed knowledge with Skills

Rather than putting all specialized knowledge into the system prompt, this approach loads it only when needed. Including every skill guide (data structure checking, README generation, skill creation, system prompt writing, tool creation) would add over 20K tokens, load unnecessary information into the Coder agent on every call, and force a redeploy to add a skill.

Deep Insight’s Skills system loads only a skill catalog of about 500 tokens at startup, with the skill list holding only names and brief descriptions. When a user requests “Create a README file,” the agent decides “I need the readme-generator skill” and calls skill_tool(skill_name="readme-generator"). The SkillLoader reads readme-generator/SKILL.md and returns a detailed guide of about 3K tokens.

# 1. Skill Discovery (at initialization)
from src.utils.skills.skill_utils import initialize_skills
available_skills, skill_prompt = initialize_skills(
    skill_dirs=["./skills"],
    verbose=True
)

# 2. Add to System Prompt (~500-token catalog)
system_prompt = base_prompt + skill_prompt

# 3. Runtime -- Agent loads skill when needed
# Agent decides: "This is README generation, I need the readme-generator skill"
# -> skill_tool(skill_name="readme-generator")
# -> Returns full SKILL.md content (~3K tokens)

Each skill is defined as a SKILL.md file composed of YAML frontmatter and detailed markdown guide. It includes metadata like name, description, license, and allowed-tools, along with Overview, When to Use This Skill, detailed instructions, and Best Practices. To add a new skill, create a new directory under skills/ and write a SKILL.md file, and it is automatically discovered.

At startup, the agent loads a skill catalog of about 500 tokens instead of wasting over 20,000 tokens on full guides (about 97 percent less). When needed, it can load an additional few thousand tokens’ worth of detailed instructions for skills.

4. Verifying quality with verification agents and safeguards

Even with Layers 1–3, one risk remains: isolated agents can’t see each other’s work, so if the Coder miscalculates, the Reporter carries that error into the report. Layer 4 is the final line of defense.

“Provide testing tools so the agent can self-verify features and fix bugs that aren’t obvious from the code alone. Have the model commit its progress to git with descriptive commit messages and write progress summaries in a progress file.”

— Anthropic, “Effective Harnesses for Long-Running Agents” (2025.11)

Implementation detail 4-1: Tracker, Validator, and Auditor agents: progress tracking and quality assurance

Tracker updates the plan’s checklist in real time. When the Coder completes data loading, the Supervisor calls Tracker, which updates the plan item from [ ] to [x] based on information like “Data load complete (1,000 rows, 5 columns).” This helps both users and the system know exactly where progress stands.

Validator independently re-executes the Coder’s calculations to verify accuracy. It reads calculation_metadata.json, re-performs each calculation from source data, and compares: matches within 0.01 pass, mismatches are flagged. Verified calculations go to citations.json for the Reporter to cite. After the Reporter finishes, the Auditor checks the final DOCX against citations.json and calculation_metadata.json without modifying them. It records citation defects in audit_findings.json and can request up to two targeted retries from the Reporter.

Implementation detail 4-2: Prioritizing calculations for verification

Verifying every calculation is inefficient, so scope the verification by importance. Deep Insight’s OptimizedValidator applies the following thresholds:

  • Over 50 calculations: aggressive filtering, verify all high plus only 10 medium.
  • Over 20 calculations: moderate filtering, verify all high plus 15 medium.
  • 20 or fewer calculations: verify most, all high plus all medium plus 5 low.

It also applies type-safe comparison: to avoid numpy-versus-Python type issues, all values are converted to float() and checked for an absolute difference under 0.01:

# validator.md -- type-safe numerical comparison
try:
    match = abs(float(expected) - float(actual)) < 0.01
except:
    match = str(expected) == str(actual)

Implementation detail 4-3: SummarizingConversationManager: the last safety net

Context can still overflow in exceptional cases, so keep a safety net under the other layers. Deep Insight uses the SummarizingConversationManager in the Strands Agents SDK for this.

# strands_sdk_utils.py -- safety net configuration at agent creation
agent = Agent(
    model=llm,
    system_prompt=system_prompts,
    tools=tools,
    conversation_manager=SummarizingConversationManager(
        summary_ratio=0.5,  # summarize oldest 50% on overflow
        preserve_recent_messages=10,  # always preserve 10 most recent messages
        summarization_system_prompt=apply_prompt_template("summarization", {})
    )
)

On overflow, the LLM summarizes the oldest 50 percent of messages into one, while always preserving the 10 most recent to keep the current task’s context. The summarization prompt (summarization.md) requires clues, plans, and tracking status to be preserved verbatim.

Implementation detail 4-4: Selective prompt caching for cost optimization

Context engineering covers cost optimization, not only token savings. Enable prompt caching per agent, based on how often each is called with the same prompt. Deep Insight’s per-agent settings:

Agent Prompt Cache Tool Cache Reason
Supervisor Yes Yes High frequency of repeated calls, with a large system prompt and tool definitions
Coder Yes Yes Running multiple analysis scripts sequentially, with the same prompt each time
Reporter Yes Yes Generating a report incrementally section by section, with high prompt-reuse frequency
Auditor Yes Yes Inspects the DOCX and JSON files over many turns with the same prompt and tools, and reruns after each Reporter retry
Coordinator No No A single one-off call, no caching benefit
Planner No No Called once per request, and again only when the user requests a plan revision
Validator No No Called with different data each time, low cache hit rate
Tracker No No Lightweight task, no tools, caching unnecessary

Agents with caching enabled insert cache points into system prompts and tool definitions, reducing input token costs by up to 90 percent on repeated calls. This is a feature natively supported by the Strands Agents SDK. Plan Reviewer does not appear in the table because it’s a human-in-the-loop step that collects user approval or feedback rather than calling a model.

Conclusion

This post has detailed the four-layer engineering approach you can use to efficiently manage context for complex tasks that exceed the context window.

  • Layer 1 (architecture-level isolation): Each agent works in an independent context through multi-agent architecture, passing only compressed summaries.
  • Layer 2 (prompt-based control): Output token budgets, standardized response formats, and self-contained code philosophy actively limit context inflow.
  • Layer 3 (filesystem use): write_and_execute_tool keeps code outside context, the filesystem serves as an inter-agent communication bus, and knowledge is lazy-loaded only when needed.
  • Layer 4 (verification and safeguards): Validator’s independent calculation re-verification, Auditor’s read-only citation audit of the final report, Tracker’s progress tracking, SummarizingConversationManager’s overflow prevention, and selective prompt caching manage both quality and cost.

Each layer forms a defense system that compensates for what the preceding layers miss. When architecture isolation is insufficient, prompts limit output. When prompts are insufficient, tools keep content external. And when problems still arise, verification catches them.

Each of these layers is documented in Anthropic’s engineering posts, “Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents”, “Code Execution with MCP”, and “How We Built Our Multi-Agent Research System”. Much of what they recommend already ships in the Strands Agents SDK rather than being something you build: SummarizingConversationManager, prompt caching, and the agents-as-tools pattern.

When building production agents, the LLM’s context window alone is rarely enough. Apply these context engineering techniques to manage context efficiently and scale your agents for production workloads.

Deep Insight, the reference implementation used here, is open source. Review the code and extend it for your domain.
