item.title: How Indegene is modernizing and scaling enterprise data quality in life sciences
item.dc:creator: Bhagyashree Chandak
item.description: This post explores how Indegene built a production-grade, LLM-powered Data Quality Agent in its NEXT Unified Data Platform on AWS. The agent generates context-aware data quality rules, validates them, and produces ready-to-run SQL and Python under human-in-the-loop governance, helping life sciences organizations scale enterprise data quality.
item.content:encoded:
This post is co-written with Shravan K S from Indegene Limited.

Enterprise AI is creating new opportunities for life sciences organizations to improve decision-making across commercial, medical, market access, and other business functions. But the quality of every AI model, dashboard, and business insight depends on one thing: trusted data. As enterprise data grows across multiple platforms, pipelines, and business domains, maintaining consistent data quality has become increasingly difficult. Manual data quality rule creation, fragmented governance, and evolving business definitions make it challenging to scale data quality across the enterprise.

This post explores how Indegene built a production-grade, large language model (LLM) powered Data Quality Agent within its NEXT Unified Data Platform (NEXT UDP) on AWS. The agent generates context-aware data quality rules, validates them, and produces ready-to-run SQL and Python code under centralized, human-in-the-loop governance. Together, these capabilities help organizations improve data quality at enterprise scale while reducing the effort required to build and maintain data quality programs.

About Indegene

Indegene Limited (BSE: 544172, NSE: INDGN) is the strategic operating partner to the life sciences industry, orchestrating commercial, medical, R&D, and safety operations across the product lifecycle. Trusted by the world’s top 20 biopharma companies, Indegene helps run complex, highly regulated workflows at global scale. Indegene combines deep life sciences expertise with AI-embedded platforms and governed operating models to improve speed, consistency, and compliance across mission-critical operations. By integrating technology into how work is executed and scaled, Indegene helps life sciences organizations deliver measurable outcomes in regulated environments.

Why conventional data quality programs break down

Most organizations have established data quality processes but keeping them effective is becoming increasingly difficult as enterprise data ecosystems evolve.

One of the biggest challenges is the divide between technical and business rule ownership. Data engineers typically define technical rules that confirm whether data is structurally correct. For example, verifying that an HCP ID (Healthcare Professional ID) isn’t null, follows the required format, is unique, and maps to a valid reference record. Business teams define rules that determine whether the data makes sense in its operational context. For example, confirming that product market share totals 100 percent within a territory or that an HCP’s prescription activity aligns with their specialty and eligibility criteria. Because technical rules are often maintained in code while business rules reside in glossaries, SOPs, and subject-matter expertise, keeping them aligned and consistently governed across datasets and platforms becomes difficult.

Traditional validation techniques also have inherent limitations. Checks for null values, data types, uniqueness, or referential integrity remain essential, but they can’t capture business-specific context. Validating product hierarchies, customer segmentation, territory alignment, or commercial business rules requires domain knowledge that static validation logic can’t easily represent.

Creating and maintaining data quality rules is equally demanding. Every new dataset requires data profiling, rule definition, SQL development, validation, and ongoing maintenance. These rules are often spread across SQL scripts, pipeline code, spreadsheets, data catalogs, and tool-specific configurations. As schemas, business definitions, or validation thresholds change, the effort required to update and govern these rules grows significantly.

Additionally, the operational impact is significant. Onboarding new datasets becomes slower because many activities are repeated manually. Maintaining quality rules across hundreds of datasets consumes valuable engineering effort. Business users lose confidence when validation rules are difficult to understand, trace, or relate to business context.

As a result, data quality often becomes a periodic governance activity rather than a continuous, scalable capability.

Rethinking data quality with generative AI

Traditional data quality tools often operate as standalone capabilities, disconnected from the broader enterprise data ecosystem. As organizations scale AI and analytics, data quality needs to be embedded within the data platform itself, where governance, metadata, lineage, and analytics work together.

Indegene addresses this through the NEXT Unified Data Platform (NEXT UDP), a modern, AI-driven data platform built specifically for life sciences. NEXT UDP brings together fragmented commercial, medical, clinical, and enterprise data into a single, governed environment so organizations can manage the complete data lifecycle from ingestion to analytics. NEXT UDP provides several standalone AI agents, such as the Data Ingestion agent, Data Quality agent, Orchestration agent, Data Catalog agent, and SQL Bot Generator agent. You can use them standalone within your data pipelines or customize them further for agent-to-agent communication.

By integrating data ingestion, transformation, data quality, governance, metadata management, and analytics within a unified platform, NEXT UDP helps organizations:

  • Consolidate fragmented enterprise data into a trusted source of truth.
  • Standardize data quality and governance across business domains.
  • Improve metadata visibility, lineage, and traceability.
  • Reduce manual effort across data engineering workflows.
  • Deliver trusted, AI-ready data for enterprise analytics and decision-making.

Figure 1: NEXT Unified Data Platform dashboard with use cases and AI agents

Figure 2: NEXT UDP technical architecture on AWS

Indegene’s life sciences clients needed an agent that could run reliably in production and meet strict governance requirements, while giving the team flexibility in how they build it. Within NEXT UDP, Generative AI powers an intelligent Data Quality Agent that augments existing data quality processes. The agent boosts data engineer and data steward productivity by accelerating rule creation, simplifying validation, and helping maintain consistent governance at enterprise scale.

Indegene built the Data Quality Agent on a set of AWS services, with Amazon Bedrock, Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore at its core. Amazon Bedrock, provides a choice of foundation models (FMs), built on a foundation of security, privacy, and responsible AI controls. For life sciences organizations, this matters because their data often includes sensitive healthcare professional and patient information. Strands Agents streamlines building and updating the agent, and its evaluation tools help Indegene test rule accuracy, which is critical in regulated life sciences environments. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The solution also inherits existing AWS security and audit controls, so Indegene can focus on data quality logic instead of agent infrastructure.

What makes the Data Quality Agent unique? Two knowledge bases that power context-aware data quality

Any data quality tool can check for null values, duplicates, or invalid data types. Services such as AWS Glue Data Quality, a capability of AWS Glue, already recommend rules like these from data statistics, and they remain a strong foundation. The harder problem is determining whether the data makes sense for its business purpose. To address this, the Data Quality Agent uses two complementary knowledge bases that combine curated domain knowledge with experience gained from governed usage.

The first is an Internal Enterprise knowledge base: It combines internal business glossaries, data dictionaries, SOPs, regulatory guidance, approved data quality rules, validated scripts, profiling results, historical anomalies, and subject matter expert (SME) feedback. Content is ingested, vectorized, and retrieved through Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) to generate data quality rules grounded in enterprise standards and proven outcomes.

The second is an External Reference knowledge base: It’s built and periodically updated using approved standardized data quality frameworks, web search, and controlled web-scraping. When a dataset is selected, the agent analyzes table and column metadata and retrieves relevant data quality standards, reference values, and validation best practices from trusted sources. For example, for an NPI (National Provider Identifier) column, it can identify applicable quality standards, recommend format (the required 10-digit numeric format) and perform reference-validation checks.

How it works

Figure 3: Data Quality Agent process flow

The Data Quality Agent takes users from data profiling to rule creation and governance in a single workflow:

  1. Select source: Connect to a supported source such as Amazon Redshift or Snowflake.
  2. Select database and schema: Browse the available tables, with the rule count and active rule status for each.
  3. Profile data: The solution computes quality metrics and column patterns for the table, which users review.
  4. Detect anomalies: The solution flags anomalies against historical baselines, and users review the total, critical, and warning issues and the affected records.
  5. Manage rules: Review a table’s existing rules or start creating new ones.
  6. Choose rule mode: Pick Column Level, Table Level, or Custom Query.
  7. Generate rule suggestions: The agent uses metadata, profiling results, anomalies, existing rules, and knowledge base context to recommend technical and business rules, each with a severity.
  8. Review, refine and apply: Users edit or approve each recommendation.
  9. Generate and validate code: The agent produces SQL and Python for approved rules, and a validation step checks them.
  10. Store in the central rule repository: Approved rules become available for execution, monitoring, and audit.

Solution architecture of the generative AI-powered Data Quality Agent on AWS

The following diagram shows the end-to-end architecture of the Data Quality Agent on the NEXT UDP platform, from the data steward request to rule execution.

Figure 4: Solution architecture of the Data Quality Agent on NEXT UDP

Data stewards and data quality analysts call the solution from the Indegene application. The following table provides a walkthrough of the solution pipeline and lists the AWS services used for each layer. It also captures other options the solution supports, so you can adapt it to your data volumes, existing tools, and operational preferences.

Layer AWS / platform services Also supported Role
API and access AWS WAF, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon Cognito – Data stewards and data quality analysts call the solution through Amazon API Gateway. AWS WAF filters requests before they reach the API, and Amazon Cognito authenticates users with OAuth 2.0 and validates the JWT on each request.
Data source layer Amazon Redshift Snowflake connector, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), JDBC/ODBC sources Provides structured and semi-structured data for data quality profiling and rule execution.
Metadata catalog layer AWS Glue Data Catalog AWS Glue crawlers for automatic schema discovery Captures databases, schemas, tables, columns, data types, and rule coverage.
Profiling and anomaly detection layer AWS Lambda (Python), with results stored in Amazon DynamoDB AWS Glue jobs, Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift SQL

Column statistics, such as null rates, distinct counts, data type conformance, patterns, value ranges and table-level signals are computed by a Python-based profiling process on AWS Lambda,

The same Lambda performs anomaly detection using statistical comparison against historical baselines to flag unexpected shifts, such as a null-rate spike or a cardinality change.
Knowledge/RAG layer Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base with Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL (pgvector) and S3 for storing knowledge documents exposed as tools through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for vector store, Amazon S3 Vectors, a capability of Amazon S3 Retrieves from the Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases (external reference standards and internal enterprise knowledge). AgentCore Gateway connects the agent to its knowledge bases as tools.
LLM intelligence layer Strands Agents on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Claude Sonnet 4.5 on Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, AgentCore memory Other foundation models available in Amazon Bedrock Generates data quality rules and uses the assembled context and few-shot prompting to recommend both technical checks (completeness, format, uniqueness) and pharma-specific business rules. Amazon Bedrock provides a choice of FMs to generate rules. AgentCore runtime provides a managed, session-isolated environment, AgentCore memory retains reviewer feedback to improve future recommendations.
Orchestration and human review layer AWS Step Functions, AWS Lambda, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), Amazon EventBridge – Coordinates profiling, LLM calls, rule generation, rule execution, status updates, and human review.
Rule metadata repository Amazon DynamoDB Amazon Aurora / Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) Stores rule ID, name, type, column, status, author, created date, severity, and version details.
Code generation, validation and storage Amazon Bedrock – Claude Sonnet 4.5 and AgentCore Code Interpreter, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with approved scripts store in Amazon S3 – Generates Python / SQL code and checks before storage
Execution layer AWS Lambda AWS Glue jobs, Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift SQL Runs data quality checks and writes violation counts and detailed anomalies.
Monitoring and dashboard layer Amazon CloudWatch, AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore or application UI Amazon Quick, Amazon OpenSearch Dashboards Data quality dashboard displays the rules applied and their status, along with total anomalies, critical anomalies, checks run, and issue details.
Security and governance AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM), AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS), AWS Secrets Manager, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Config, Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub, Amazon Inspector, virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoints – Authentication, encryption, secrets, audit, and threat detection

How the Data Quality Agent builds context

Before recommending any validation rule, the Data Quality Agent assembles context from six distinct sources, each answering a different question about the data:

Context Source What it provides Question it answers
Table/Column Metadata (Catalog) Schema, data types from the Data Catalog What is this data?
Data Profile Column-level statistics computed from the actual data, such as null rates, distinct counts, value ranges, frequent values and detected patterns What does the data look like right now?
Anomaly Detection Results Unexpected changes flagged by comparing the latest profile with historical baselines, such as a sudden rise in nulls, a change in distinct values, or out-of-range values What has changed or looks wrong?
Existing Active Data Quality Rules Rules already applied at the table or column level, retrieved from the rule repository What rules already exist, so we don’t duplicate or conflict?
External Reference Knowledge Base Universal, publicly established data quality standards and validation best practices (for example, format and structural rules for identifiers like the National Provider Identifier) What are the industry standards for this field?
Internal Enterprise Knowledge Base Organization-specific data quality rule patterns, prior reviewer feedback, and curated business/technical rule libraries How does this organization define quality?

Together, these sources let the agent reason like an experienced data steward. Grounding every recommendation in what the data is, what the standards require, how the enterprise defines quality, and what has already been implemented.

What the solution does

The Data Quality Agent generates several categories of checks and keeps data stewards in control of the results.

Anomaly checks generation

The solution generates anomaly checks that catch values which are technically valid but don’t match how a pharmaceutical market behaves. These include negative switch percentages, market shares that don’t add up to 100 percent within a market, inconsistent drug rankings (for example, a drug ranked first with a lower share than the drug ranked second), rating values outside the defined scale, and panel sizes that are too small or don’t match the number of respondents.

Context-aware rule generation with RAG

The Data Quality Agent generates rule recommendations in three modes:

Rule Type Description
Column Level Generates data quality rules for a specific, individual column selected by the user. The agent reads that column’s metadata and profiling signals to suggest checks such as data type validation, null and mandatory-field checks, length and range validation, pattern/format validation, and uniqueness.
Table Level Generates data quality rules for the table as a whole, driven by the table’s metadata and relationships across its columns. This covers record consistency, duplicate detection, cross-column validation, referential integrity checks, and table-wide business consistency.
Custom Query Generates SQL-based rules from natural language input. The user describes the business validation in plain English and the agent produces the corresponding SQL, which can then be refined conversationally or edited directly to support complex validations that fall outside standard column and table checks.

The Create New Quality Rule interface provides dedicated Column Level, Table Level, and Custom Query modes.

The platform supports both technical validation and business-specific quality checks.

For technical rules, the agent generates checks that confirm the data is structurally sound. These include null checks for mandatory fields, data type validation, range validation for numeric and date values, pattern validation for formatted fields such as identifiers and codes, duplicate detection, and referential integrity checks between related tables.

For business rules, the agent generates life sciences checks that confirm the data is consistent with how the business operates. These include account affiliation consistency (for example, a healthcare provider linked to the correct organization), segmentation logic, eligibility criteria, and market share and product share validation (for example, shares within a territory not exceeding 100%).

Real use-case example

Consider an HCP Product Performance table with the columns HCP_ID, Specialty, Territory_ID, Product_ID, Prescription_Volume, Market_Share_Pct, Switch_Pct, Rating_Scale, and Reporting_Month. Using the table profile and the two Knowledge Bases, this is how the Data Quality Agent generates and performs the following checks:

  1. Anomaly checks performed.
    • Negative switch percentage.
    • Market share total mismatch.
    • Sudden increase or decrease in prescription volume.
    • Inconsistent product rankings.
    • Invalid rating-scale values.
  2. Technical rules generated.
    • HCP_ID must not be null or duplicated.
    • Prescription_Volume must be numeric and non-negative.
    • Market_Share_Pct and Switch_Pct must be between 0 and 100.
    • Reporting_Month must follow the required date format.
    • Territory_ID and Product_ID must match their reference tables.
  3. Business rules generated.
    • Market share across all products must total 100 percent for each territory and reporting month.
    • The HCP’s product eligibility must align with their specialty.
    • Only eligible HCPs can be included in the target segment.

AI-assisted severity recommendation

The solution recommends severity based on dataset context, rule type, and business impact. Severity categories help distinguish between:

  • Critical issues, such as invalid commercial metrics, incorrect identifiers, or business rule violations.
  • Basic validations, including schema conformance, null checks, and length validation.
  • Complex validations involving advanced SQL logic, multi-column rules, or domain-specific business checks.
  • Information: Validation conducted for awareness and transparency purposes only. No action is required unless concerns are identified.

SQL/Python code generation and ETL integration

After a rule is approved, the LLM generates the equivalent SQL, Python, and PySpark code. Before it’s stored, the code is validated automatically with syntax checks, a check against the target schema, and a test run on sample data where the language supports it. This means existing extract, transform, and load (ETL) and orchestration tools can run them as part of the current data pipelines.

AI-assisted validation

Using an LLM as a Validation Agent to review data quality (DQ) rules/scripts generated by another LLM for reducing hallucinations and improving governance. Further, Amazon Bedrock provides security, privacy, and responsible AI controls. Prompts and outputs aren’t used to train the models or shared with model providers. Amazon Bedrock is HIPAA eligible and in scope for compliance programs such as SOC, ISO and GDPR, which helps Indegene meet the requirements of its life sciences clients. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails adds configurable safeguards on model inputs and outputs. It detects and masks personally identifiable information (PII), blocks harmful content and prompt injection attacks, and uses contextual grounding checks to flag responses that aren’t supported by the retrieved knowledge.

Human oversight remains central

The Data Quality Agent is designed to augment existing data quality processes. Each generated rule receives a confidence score. Only high-confidence, low-risk rules are approved automatically, while critical and business rules always go to an SME for review. Every decision is recorded in the rule repository, so rule management stays governed, traceable, and aligned with enterprise standards.

Delivering operational impact and business value

In production, across Indegene’s deployments of NEXT UDP for life sciences clients, the Data Quality Agent has reduced the effort to define and implement data quality rules from about 30 hours to about 4 hours per dataset. That’s roughly 85 percent less effort, or about 7x higher productivity. Onboarding a new table now takes 2–4 hours instead of 2–5 working days. Data engineers and data stewards now spend their time reviewing and approving rules rather than writing them from scratch.

Key outcomes include:

  • Less manual effort through AI-generated rules, SQL, and Python.
  • Faster onboarding of new tables, schemas, and business domains.
  • More consistent rules, grounded in approved standards, enterprise knowledge, and existing rules.
  • Better collaboration between business and technical teams through the review, refine, and approve workflow.
  • Earlier detection of data quality issues through automated profiling and anomaly detection.

Table 1: Performance and Scale

Metric Impact*
Enterprise profiling 25–50 schemas; 500–2,000 tables; 10,000–50,000 columns
Table profiling 45–90 sec (~1M rows); 2–5 min (~10M rows)
AI rule generation 20–45 sec per table
SQL generation 3–8 sec per rule; 20–60 sec for 10–15 rules
Rule execution 20–30 sec (standard); 1–3 min (complex SQL)
Central rule repository 1,000–10,000 rules
DQ checks per execution 100–500 per domain. Scalable to 1,000+

*Estimated from Indegene’s production deployments

Table 2: Rule quality and validation

Metric Impact* What does it mean
Rule suggestion accuracy 80–90% Suggestions that are technically valid and apply correctly to the column or table
Rule acceptance rate 60–75% Suggestions approved without any changes
Rule refinement rate / Human Override Rate 20–35% Suggestions approved after the reviewer edited logic or thresholds
SQL validity 90–97% (schema-grounded); 80–90% (custom SQL) Generated SQL that passes validation on the first attempt
Severity recommendation accuracy 75–85% Recommended severity matching the reviewer’s final severity
Business relevance (SME rating) 4.0–4.5 / 5 SME rating of how useful the recommended rules are to the business
Hallucination rate <5–8% Suggestions that reference non-existent columns or incorrect business logic

*Estimated from Indegene’s production deployments

Table 3: Operational efficiency

Metric Impact*
Manual SQL rule authoring 60–80% reduction in end-to-end effort, including review and refinement
New table onboarding 2–5 working days → 2–4 hours
Rule reuse 40–60% of new rules adapted from existing approved rules
LLM cost optimization Up to 90% lower input-token cost on cached context with Amazon Bedrock prompt caching
Compute optimization ~45–51% reduction with metadata-first profiling

*Estimated from Indegene’s production deployments

Table 4: Manual compared to agent-assisted data quality

Activity Traditional DQ Approach Generative AI-powered DQ approach Impact*
Rule Discovery Manual review of schemas, profiling reports, sample data, and documentation. Existing tools can generate basic profiling checks but often miss domain-specific business logic Agent uses metadata, profiling results, table context, existing rule patterns, and optional business descriptions to recommend technical and life sciences-specific data quality rules 80-85% faster
Technical Rule Generation Manual creation of null, data type, range, uniqueness, and integrity rules Automated rule generation with human review 80-85% faster
Business Rule Definition Validation is often based on technical metadata with limited understanding of product, segment, customer, or eligibility logic. Business context depends heavily on SME discussions and manual translation into validation logic Uses RAG to retrieve business glossaries, data dictionaries, existing rules, and historical anomaly patterns to generate context-aware recommendations. 70-75% faster
Rules authoring and SQL/Python Development Engineers manually define validation rules and perform coding, debugging, and testing for each dataset or business requirement. Auto-generated rules at the Column Level, Table Level, and Custom Query levels, and generate SQL/Python for the selected DQ checks. Users can review, refine, and apply the recommendations. 80-85% faster to first working code
Rule Validation Rules are validated manually, involving multiple iterations of executing the queries and refining Agent scores, refines, and optimizes rules automatically 80-85% faster
Rule Reuse Manual copy, modify, and reuse Approved rules and feedback added to the agent’s knowledge 50% faster onboarding for new datasets in an existing domain
Anomaly Detection Manual analysis of profiling outputs and records Automated anomaly detection with business-context explanations 80-85% faster
Severity classification Rule severity and business impact are determined manually, which can lead to inconsistent prioritization. Recommends severity based on rule type, dataset context, and business impact. Consistent, context-based severity
Governance & Traceability Rules are often distributed across tools, scripts, spreadsheets, or catalogs, making governance and traceability difficult. Approval and review workflows vary across teams. Central, versioned rule repository with ownership 85% reduction in maintenance effort
Human Effort SMEs and engineers drive every step SMEs focus on review and approval. The agent handles discovery and generation Higher productivity & scalability, ~7x productivity

*Estimated from Indegene’s production deployments

Looking ahead

As enterprise data ecosystems continue to grow, maintaining consistent and scalable data quality becomes increasingly difficult using manual rule creation and fragmented governance processes. Generative AI provides an opportunity to augment these workflows by accelerating rule generation, incorporating business context, and supporting governed decision-making.

The generative AI-powered Data Quality Agent within the NEXT Unified Data Platform demonstrates how large language models, RAG, and centralized rule governance can work together to simplify data quality management while keeping humans in control of review and approval. Future enhancements will continue to build on this foundation, including:

  • AI-assisted remediation recommendations to help users resolve failed data quality checks.
  • Root cause analysis to identify recurring anomaly patterns and support faster investigation of repeated data quality issues.

As these capabilities evolve, the focus remains the same: helping organizations improve data quality through AI-assisted automation while maintaining governance, transparency, and business oversight.

item.title: How U Mobile built agentic telco operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.dc:creator: Jin Tiong Lim
item.description: U Mobile, Malaysia's newest 5G network provider, built AiDaH, an agentic AI operations platform on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that moves beyond AI assistance to autonomous action across telco operations. Nine months after production launch, AiDaH handles over 150 operational scenarios across six divisions, cutting trouble tickets by up to 84.5%.
item.content:encoded:
U Mobile, Malaysia’s newest 5G network provider, has always run its telco operations lean, doing more with less through continuous automation. When new AI capabilities became available, U Mobile explored how to enhance operational efficiency beyond basic productivity gains. The real opportunity was further upstream, in how operations teams diagnose and resolve problems in the first place. The same lean operating discipline shaped the foundation for AiDaH: not a one-off technology initiative, but the next step in a long-running journey to simplify operations and scale capability without adding complexity.

When a subscriber can’t purchase a data add-on, resolving it isn’t a single problem. It’s a coordination problem. A customer service agent needs to pull interface logs for error codes. The same agent must then query business support system APIs for subscriber eligibility, and cross-reference internal knowledge bases for applicable business policies. All of that happens across multiple systems, before drafting a single word of response. And when that fails, the ticket escalates to backend IT teams and the subscriber waits even longer.

Traditional automation tools can help agents write better responses. What they can’t do is navigate multiple systems, analyze the results, and propose corrective action. Closing that gap takes an agentic architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

U Mobile’s Information Systems Division (ISD) built exactly that. Working with AWS and AWS Partner Axrail, they created AiDaH, the AI-Driven Agentic Helpdesk, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Two capabilities decided the choice. The managed agent runtime meant there was no agent infrastructure to operate. Built-in memory carried conversational context across turns without standing up a separate state store. Within a year of starting the journey, AiDaH handles over 150 documented operational scenarios across six business divisions. U Mobile’s internal measurements show trouble ticket volumes falling by up to 84.5 percent in key categories.

In this post, we walk through the six-layer architecture behind AiDaH. We then describe the security foundation beneath the platform, and close with a brief note on the spec-driven method the team used to build it.

The problem: Too many systems, too much friction

U Mobile’s IT landscape reflects the complexity typical of modern telecommunications: business support and customer relationship management systems, mobile number portability platforms, big data analytics, and infrastructure monitoring tools, running hybrid across on-premises and cloud.

Before AiDaH, this fragmentation meant that even routine diagnoses required manually checking logs, querying subscriber eligibility, and consulting knowledge bases for business policies, across separate systems and portals. Each lookup was a context switch, each context switch was time lost, and each unresolved query became an escalation to a backend IT team. Expanding coverage to additional operational domains compounded the problem, because every new system typically required a bespoke integration.

The ISD team’s strategy rested on three pillars.

  1. Reach: agents that coordinate across backend systems in real time.
  2. Depth: chain-of-thought reasoning for multi-step root cause analysis.
  3. Community: a secure multi-tenant framework with role-based access control and built-in guardrails, available to every division.

The journey: From knowledge base to agentic platform

AiDaH started with a principle: think big, start small. U Mobile began conceptualization in late 2025 with two pilot agents and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, a fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability. A Q1 2026 pilot brought the internal IT helpdesk online with 4 agents and 20 operational scenarios. Through 2026 the platform hardened and expanded, adding three-tier routing and reaching 6 agents by mid-year. AiDaH went live to 50 L2 call center and branch users in Q3 2026 with 8 agents, and now covers more than 150 documented operational scenarios.

What agentic means in practice

The difference between traditional AI assistance and agentic AI is best illustrated through a real example.

With a traditional AI assistant, a support agent handling “mobile data not working overseas” gets help drafting a response and some suggested troubleshooting steps, but still manually checks roaming status, verifies eligibility, raises tickets, and sends the final reply.

With AiDaH, the system independently checks the subscriber’s roaming configuration, verifies international data eligibility, and identifies the specific point of failure. It then assembles a remediation plan: which services to reset, what configuration to push, and whether a network ticket is warranted. The support agent reviews and confirms, and the actions execute. The investigation that used to consume the agent’s time now happens before they read the first line. The human decision point is preserved where it matters: at the moment something changes on a live subscriber account.

In one production case, a subscriber reported being unable to purchase an add-on. AiDaH traced the failure to an error code, “Subscriber has pending order.” It also revealed that the customer had attempted the same purchase more than 30 times across multiple channels over three days, every attempt blocked by the same underlying pending order. AiDaH surfaced the root cause and the remediation steps in a single response. Previously that would have required manual investigation across several systems.

Architecture: Six layers, one interface

AiDaH runs on a layered architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, deployed in the Asia Pacific (Singapore) Region. Staff interact through Microsoft Teams, a deliberate choice to meet most users where they already work, with no new application to learn and no portal switching.

The following diagram shows how the layers fit together.

Figure 1: AiDaH’s layered architecture

As shown in Figure 1, the platform is organized into six layers.

Layer 1: Staff interface

Staff reach AiDaH through Microsoft Teams and a web portal served by Amazon CloudFront and protected by AWS WAF, with an AWS Lambda backend and a REST API for programmatic triggers.

Layer 2: Orchestration

The routing brain on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Every request passes a pre-flight security check covering role-based access control, identity validation, and guardrails, then enters a cost-optimized routing tier. Roughly 70 percent of requests resolve through deterministic keyword matching with no model invocation, 20 percent are classified by a lightweight model, and only 10 percent require the full orchestrator. The cheapest path that can confidently handle the request is the one that runs.

Layer 3: Specialist agents

Eight experts spanning customer relationship management, customer problem management, number portability, order and SIM operations, infrastructure monitoring, big data analytics, cloud cost management, and finance operations. They communicate over the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, which lets them delegate subtasks and complete cross-system workflows no single agent could handle alone.

Layer 4: Gateways and backend APIs

AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, exposes U Mobile’s backends to agents through a unified Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface. Behind each gateway sit AWS Lambda functions and MCP servers that translate agent intent into calls against a specific system.

Layer 5: Data and knowledge

Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed RAG capability, grounds agent responses in governed content, using an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector store. Content spans a shared enterprise knowledge base and a separate finance corpus. AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, maintains conversational context across turns, and Amazon DynamoDB holds the six-tier role-based access control model and session metadata.

Layer 6: Operational systems

U Mobile’s on-premises and cloud operational systems are reached over AWS Transit Gateway and AWS Site-to-Site VPN, an IPsec-encrypted tunnel with no public internet exposure.

How a request flows through the layers

Tracing a single request makes the interaction between the layers concrete. Consider a support agent who types a port-in status question into the AiDaH channel in Microsoft Teams.

  1. Interface: The Teams message reaches an AWS Lambda function, which forwards the request and the caller’s federated identity to the orchestrator.
  2. Pre-flight check: The orchestrator resolves the caller against the six-tier role-based access control model held in Amazon DynamoDB, validates the token issued by AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and applies Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to the incoming prompt. A request that fails any of these checks stops here.
  3. Routing: The orchestrator selects the cheapest tier that can handle the request. A recognized phrase such as “port-in status” matches deterministically and skips model invocation entirely. An ambiguous phrasing goes to the lightweight classifier. A novel or multi-part question goes to the full orchestrator.
  4. Agent instantiation: The selected specialist agent runs as a session in AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore memory rehydrates the conversation so the agent inherits the subscriber number and any prior findings from earlier turns, instead of asking the user to repeat them.
  5. Tool discovery and invocation: The agent queries AgentCore Gateway for the tools it is entitled to use. Each gateway publishes its backend as MCP tools with typed inputs and outputs, so the agent picks a tool by name and schema rather than by hand-coded integration logic. Amazon Cognito brokers the OAuth authorization for the call.
  6. Backend call: The gateway’s Lambda function or MCP server translates the tool call into a request against the target system, traversing AWS Transit Gateway and the Site-to-Site VPN tunnel to reach the on-premises number portability platform. Sensitive fields are masked on the way back, before the response reaches the model.
  7. Reasoning and collaboration: If the answer spans domains, the agent delegates over the Agent2Agent protocol. A port-in query that turns out to be a billing block, for example, hands off to the business support systems agent, and the results are merged into one narrative.
  8. Response and audit: The agent grounds its explanation against Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, then returns the finding and proposed remediation to Teams for human confirmation. AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, writes the full trace of prompts, tool calls, token counts, and latencies to Amazon CloudWatch, and AWS CloudTrail records the corresponding API activity.

Onboarding a new operational domain adds a gateway and its MCP tool definitions at step 5. Steps 1–4, and steps 7 and 8, are unchanged. The stable core is what keeps the marginal cost of each new domain low.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capabilities in production

The following table maps each AgentCore capability to the job it does in AiDaH.

Capability Role in AiDaH
Runtime Hosts AiDaH and its sub-agents as managed containers that scale automatically, with no servers to provision
Memory Maintains conversational context such as subscriber number, order IDs, and prior findings across turns
Identity Issues short-lived access tokens so only authorized users can invoke agents
Gateway Connects agents to U Mobile backends through a unified, secure MCP interface
Observability Streams every prompt, tool call, token count, and latency measurement to Amazon CloudWatch

Securing the foundation

Deploying an agentic AI platform that reaches subscriber data, billing systems and network infrastructure demands more than application-level security. It requires a secure cloud foundation. U Mobile took a two-pronged approach: validating and enhancing the underlying AWS Landing Zone, and building on the security capabilities in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

Landing Zone security – Before scaling AiDaH to production, U Mobile engaged AWS to run a Well-Architected Security Review of the Landing Zone hosting the platform. The review validated the environment against AWS security best practices. Infrastructure protection came first, through AWS Control Tower guardrails and AWS Organizations service control policies. The review then examined centralized identity federation and network security controls for ingress and egress. Consolidated security findings in AWS Security Hub and encryption standards across every architecture tier completed the assessment. The outcome was twofold: confidence that every AiDaH component operates on an independently validated foundation, and a prioritized roadmap for continuous improvement.

Application-layer security – Every agent action traces to a specific authenticated user. Staff federate through Microsoft Entra ID, and AgentCore Identity issues the short-lived token that authorizes agent invocation. Amazon Cognito brokers OAuth authorization at the gateway. An agent can therefore reach only the systems its invoking user is entitled to see. A six-tier role-based access control model enforces permissions per agent, per tool, and per data source. Sensitive subscriber data is masked at the gateway before it reaches the model, with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails enforcing content policies.

Every prompt, tool invocation and response is streamed to Amazon CloudWatch Logs through AgentCore Observability, and AWS CloudTrail records the underlying API activity. That audit trail matters: AiDaH is now written into U Mobile’s L2 support standard operating procedures and is subject to operational audit. All compute runs in private VPC subnets, on-premises connectivity is exclusively over encrypted VPN, and AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) manages encryption keys for data at rest and in transit.

Over 150 documented operational scenarios

The scenarios AiDaH covers currently span six domains. The following table summarizes the coverage in each.

Domain Coverage
Customer management Account details, billing history, payment status, active plans and contracts, SIM information, service status
Order operations and logistics Order and delivery status, pending orders, resource allocation, tracing workflows, delivery tracking, shipment history
Customer problem management Root-cause diagnosis for failed add-on purchases, plan changes and top-up failures. Number portability port-in and port-out checks. Service disruption diagnosis across SMS, calls and data
IT infrastructure operations Server and device status monitoring, IP and hostname lookups, network device inventory
Business intelligence and analytics Subscriber trend analysis, device take-up trends, revenue trending, anomaly detection, individual subscriber analytics. The analytics agent converts plain-language questions into SQL queries, so no technical skills are required
Knowledge retrieval Enterprise-wide retrieval with context-aware, grounded responses and citations back to source evidence

Measuring progress: An AI competency model

To track progress and establish a shared vocabulary across the organization, the team adopted an eight-level AI competency model, from basic digital access to autonomous self-healing operations. It draws on industry thinking, including the TM Forum Autonomous Networks maturity levels, adapted to U Mobile’s operational context. The following table lists the eight levels.

Level Name Description
1 Digital access Self-service portals, online tools and dashboards
2 Scripted automation Rules-based workflow triggers and auto-routing
3 Basic AI assistance Simple chatbots, FAQ look-ups, intent classification
4 Contextual intelligence Context-aware suggestions, basic natural language understanding with memory
5 Proactive AI Predictive alerts, anomaly detection, recommendation engines
6 Autonomous task execution AI completes defined tasks end to end with guardrails
7 Collaborative multi-agent Specialist agents collaborate, use tools, retrieve governed knowledge
8 Self-healing and adaptive Autonomous systems that detect, diagnose, remediate, and learn continuously

AiDaH reached Level 7 within nine months of the first pilot: specialist agents collaborate, use tools, retrieve governed knowledge, and support operational decision-making across domains. Level 8, where problems are detected, diagnosed, and resolved without human involvement, is the current target.

Driving adoption: From tool to teammate

Deploying AiDaH was one challenge. Getting people to trust and use it was another.

ISD recognized early that adoption isn’t a technology problem but a behavior change challenge. Staff were accustomed to established workflows, trusted tools, and familiar escalation paths. Introducing AiDaH meant asking them to change deeply embedded habits. It also meant trusting an AI to retrieve information, diagnose problems, and propose next steps on their behalf.

The team leaned on directed prompting. Rather than expecting open-ended exploration, ISD provided structured prompt templates for common scenarios. Those templates turned “ask AiDaH anything” into “here is exactly how to ask for a billing check or a port-in status.” That reduced hesitation and produced immediate, tangible results. When responses proved fast, accurate, and actionable, word spread. An internal survey rated the platform 4.6 out of 5 for ease of use, and daily use is now routine among frontline teams.

The clearest signal came when AiDaH was formally incorporated into U Mobile’s L2 support standard operating procedures. Moving from optional tool to auditable SOP is what marked the shift from experimentation to operations.

ISD’s approach was never about buying a finished solution. It was about owning the journey: building internal AI capability, encouraging responsible experimentation, and embedding practical AI fluency into the daily operating rhythm. Beyond AiDaH itself, ISD maintains a dedicated internal AI channel where teams share use cases, techniques, and early experiments. The goal isn’t to concentrate AI expertise in one team but to distribute it, so every division can use AI confidently within governed guardrails. Progress was not linear. The path involved setbacks and recalibrations, and each one made the platform and the team stronger.

Results

According to U Mobile’s internal measurements, monthly trouble ticket volumes declined across three major categories between January and September 2026:

  • Provisioning and network tickets fell 84.5 percent.
  • General inquiries dropped 81.6 percent.
  • Billing and charging reduced by 48.7 percent.

How the team built it: Spec-driven development with Kiro

U Mobile accelerated AiDaH’s development using Kiro, the AWS agentic IDE built around spec-driven development. In Kiro, a new capability begins as a spec rather than a prompt: requirements, design, and task breakdown are written down and reviewed first, and code generation works against that agreed artifact. For AiDaH, this mattered most at the agent and tool boundary. Each new operational domain means a new gateway, a set of MCP tool definitions, and the role-based access control entries that decide who might call them. Writing those down first made each new domain a repeatable unit of work rather than a fresh design exercise.

The supporting toolchain is conventional. The team used Kiro IDE for local development, with agent hooks and MCP integrations, alongside Kiro CLI for pipeline automation. Source control runs on GitLab, with AWS CodePipeline and AWS CodeBuild driving continuous integration, container images published to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), and SonarQube providing continuous code quality scanning. Specifications drove the code generation. The discipline let a small team grow from a two-use-case proof of concept to over 150 documented use cases on a 12-week sprint cadence.

Key architectural decisions

Several choices shaped how AiDaH scaled from proof of concept to production platform. Four stand out, each one reducing the cost of adding the next operational domain or keeping the platform governable as it grew.

AgentCore as managed infrastructure – Rather than building a custom agent framework, the team used the built-in scaling, identity, memory, and observability capabilities in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AWS manages the underlying provisioning, scaling, and patching, which removed an entire layer of infrastructure engineering.

MCP for universal tool connectivity – Standardizing on the Model Context Protocol means AiDaH can onboard new backend systems without rebuilding agent logic. Each new operational domain needs a new gateway, not a new integration architecture.

A2A for specialist collaboration – The Agent2Agent protocol lets domain specialists delegate subtasks to each other. A query spanning customer records, interface logs and billing data routes naturally across the relevant agents.

Secure foundation first – Running the Well-Architected Security Review on the Landing Zone before scaling to production means security controls are inherited by every new agent and gateway, rather than bolted on afterwards.

What’s next

U Mobile’s roadmap focuses on expanding both breadth and depth: onboarding additional operational domains and backend integrations, while evolving the platform’s capabilities from single-system queries toward multi-system correlated diagnosis. The longer-term goal, Level 8 on the competency model, is to move from informing support agents to autonomously resolving issues.

Security governance matures in parallel. The team is aligning practices with NIST SP 800-53, the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, the CSA AI Trust Framework, and MITRE ATLAS. Compliance with Malaysia’s Personal Data Protection Act and Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission regulations continues alongside it.

Conclusion

AiDaH shows what changes when AI stops assisting and starts acting. In under a year, U Mobile went from a two-agent proof of concept to eight specialist agents serving over 150 documented operational scenarios. According to U Mobile’s internal measurements, trouble tickets fell by up to 84.5 percent in key categories, and U Mobile has now written the platform into its formal L2 support procedures.

We walked through the six layers, followed a request from Teams to an on-premises system and back, and described the Well-Architected Security Review that preceded the production scale up. The technical foundation mattered, but so did the less glamorous work. That meant validating the Landing Zone before scaling, writing structured prompts so staff knew how to start, and treating adoption as a behavior change problem rather than a deployment milestone. Teams facing similar system fragmentation might find the same pattern useful. Start with a managed agent runtime, add a standard tool protocol at the integration boundary, and run a security review before the scale up rather than after it.

The direction remains clear: expand securely, automate responsibly, and move steadily toward autonomous, self-healing operations, one deliberate and governed step at a time.

To learn more, visit Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide. To explore spec-driven development, see Kiro.

item.title: Bring structured and unstructured data together with Amazon Quick
item.dc:creator: Puneeth Komaragiri
item.description: Amazon Quick brings structured and unstructured data together in one experience. In this post, you connect Amazon S3 as a knowledge base, enrich a dataset, build a Space, and create a custom chat agent that answers business questions across both data types through a single conversational interface.
item.content:encoded:
Organizations collect data in many forms. Structured data lives in databases and spreadsheets, whereas unstructured data sits in documents, reports, and files stored across file systems. Analyzing both together typically requires switching between multiple tools, running separate queries, and manually correlating results.

Amazon Quick addresses this with a unified experience. You can connect structured data through enriched datasets and unstructured data through S3-backed knowledge bases. You can then query both through a single conversational AI agent.

In this post, you learn how to:

  • Connect Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) as a data source and create a knowledge base.
  • Build a Space that combines structured and unstructured data.
  • Create and configure a custom chat agent that queries across both data types.
  • Ask questions that span structured and unstructured sources in a single conversation.

Solution architecture

The following diagram illustrates how each component connects to deliver a unified data experience through Amazon Quick.

Figure 1: Solution architecture for combining structured and unstructured data in Amazon Quick

The architecture has three layers:

  • Data layer: Your data exists in two forms. Unstructured content (documents, PDFs, reports) is stored in Amazon S3 and indexed through a knowledge base. Structured data (metrics, sales figures, and operational key performance indicators) is loaded as enriched datasets with semantic descriptions that the agent uses to translate questions into SQL.
  • Workspace layer: A Space brings both data types together into a single workspace. The Space references your knowledge base for unstructured queries and your datasets for structured queries. It can also include dashboards, file uploads, and action connectors. This is the layer where data from different sources converges into a unified context.
  • Agent layer: The custom chat agent links to the Space and uses it as its knowledge source. When a user asks a question, the agent determines whether to query the knowledge base, the dataset, or both, and returns a combined response with citations. Amazon Quick also applies built-in AI guardrails, such as content safety screening, to chat interactions.

With this layered approach, you can expand the solution over time. When you add a new data source to the Space, the agent linked to that Space can use it, and responses respect the permissions of the user who asks.

Prerequisites

To follow along with this walkthrough, you need:

  • An Amazon Quick account with an Enterprise subscription for the user who follows this walkthrough (creating datasets requires Enterprise). For details, see Amazon Quick pricing.
  • An Amazon S3 bucket for your business documents. To create one, see the Amazon S3 User Guide.
  • Amazon Quick access to your S3 bucket, granted by an Amazon Quick administrator. In the admin console, the administrator chooses Permissions, then AWS resources, selects Amazon S3, and chooses Select S3 buckets. Selected buckets have read-only permissions by default.
  • Permissions to create integrations, knowledge bases, datasets, spaces, and chat agents in Amazon Quick.

Prepare your sample data

This walkthrough uses two types of data:

Unstructured documents: Upload these to your Amazon S3 bucket for the knowledge base:

  • AnyCompany_Business_Review.pdf
  • AnyCompany_Market_Analysis_Report.pdf
  • AnyCompany_Product_Strategy_Memo.pdf

Structured data: Download this file to your computer. You upload it directly to Amazon Quick in Step 3:

  • Product_Sales.csv

Step 1: Create an Amazon S3 integration

Start by connecting Amazon Quick to your S3 bucket. From the Amazon Quick console, select Knowledge in the left navigation panel.

The knowledge page shows available connector types, including Amazon Q Business, Web Crawler, Amazon S3, and third-party options like Google Drive, OneDrive, and Microsoft SharePoint.

Under Amazon S3, choose Add. In the Create S3 knowledge base dialog, on the Connect S3 bucket page, provide the following details:

  • Name: A descriptive name for your integration (for example, “My Data Access Integration”).
  • S3 bucket location: Choose Quick Suite instance account to use a bucket in the same AWS account as Amazon Quick, or Other AWS account for a bucket in a different account.
  • S3 bucket URL: The S3 URI of the bucket containing your data. The bucket must be in the same Region as Amazon Quick.

Choose Next.

Figure 2: Create integration dialog showing the S3 connection fields

Step 2: Create a knowledge base

After the S3 integration is created, Amazon Quick prompts you to create a knowledge base. The knowledge base indexes your S3 content for AI-powered search.

Configure the knowledge base:

  • Name: “Business Knowledge Base”.
  • Description (optional): Notes about how the knowledge base will be used.
  • Content: Select “Add all content” to index everything in the connected S3 bucket, or “Add specific content” to specify the S3 prefixes for the folders and files to include (prefix filters are case-sensitive).

Next: Additional settings opens optional settings for document-level access control lists (ACLs) and a metadata files folder. Decide whether to use ACLs before you create the knowledge base, because you can’t change that choice later. This walkthrough uses sample data, so the default settings are sufficient. For details, see Set up and manage Amazon S3 integration.

Choose Create. A success banner confirms the S3 integration, and the knowledge base begins indexing in the background.

Figure 3: Create knowledge base dialog with the Business Knowledge Base name and content options

Step 3: Create and enrich a dataset

A dataset is your structured data file loaded into Amazon Quick. By enriching the dataset with semantic descriptions, custom instructions, and correct data types, the AI agent can interpret your data more accurately. It can then translate natural language questions into SQL queries.

Create the dataset

  1. From the Amazon Quick home page, navigate to Data in the left navigation.
  2. Choose Create dataset, then select Upload file.
  3. Select the Product_Sales.csv file you downloaded earlier and choose Open.
  4. On the confirmation screen, review the column names and data types. Choose Next to create the dataset.

Amazon Quick ingests the file into SPICE (the in-memory calculation engine) and the dataset appears in your dataset list.

The dataset takes its name from the uploaded file, so it appears as Product_Sales.csv in your account.

Enrich the dataset

Enriching your dataset with semantic information helps the AI understand your data in business context. The agent uses this context to translate natural language questions into more accurate SQL queries. From the dataset page, choose Edit dataset to enter the data preparation view.

Transform: Fix data types

In the Transform tab, update data types for columns that were auto-detected incorrectly. For this dataset:

  • Change Order Date and Date Key from String to Date.
  • Change Customer ID from String to Integer.
  • Change Sales, Discount, and Profit from String to Decimal.
  • Change Quantity and Unit Price from String to Integer.

Figure 4: Transform view showing data type changes applied to the Product_Sales.csv dataset

Output: Add semantic context

Select the Output tab to access the dataset-level enrichment fields. Here you provide context that helps the AI understand what your data represents and how to use it.

Description: Add a dataset-level description:

“Product sales transaction data for AnyCompany, covering orders from FY2024-FY2025 across North America, EMEA, Asia Pacific, and Latin America. Includes order details, customer information, product lines, and revenue metrics.”

Custom instructions: Add guidance for how the AI should query this data:

USAGE GUIDELINES:

  • Revenue values are in USD.
  • When comparing performance, group by Region (North America, EMEA, Asia Pacific, Latin America).
  • Order Date should be used for time-based trend analysis. The fiscal year matches the calendar year.
  • Date Key is a numeric YYYYMMDD representation of Order Date.
  • Sales = Quantity x Unit Price x (1 – Discount)

COMMON USE CASES:

  • Regional sales performance comparison.
  • Product line revenue analysis.
  • Quarterly trend identification.
  • Customer segmentation by industry and segment.

TAGS: Sales, revenue, orders, regional performance, product analytics

Column descriptions: Select each column in the left panel and add a description. For example:

  • Order ID: “Unique identifier for each sales transaction (format: REGION-YYYY-NNNNNN)”
  • Region: “Geographic sales region: North America, EMEA, Asia Pacific, or Latin America”
  • Product: “AnyCompany product name: Analytics Pro, Connect, Automate, AI Assistant, Data Catalog, or Integration Hub”
  • Sales: “Order revenue in USD after discount”
  • Segment: “Customer size segment: Enterprise, Mid-Market, or SMB”

Figure 5: Output view showing dataset details with Description and Custom instructions configured

Choose Save & publish to save your changes. The dataset summary now shows the columns with their correct data types and the descriptions you added.

Figure 6: Enriched Product_Sales.csv dataset summary showing all 16 columns, data types, and descriptions

This enriched dataset provides the structured data layer for your solution. When the agent receives a natural language question about sales data, it uses these descriptions and instructions to generate more accurate SQL queries. Combined with the knowledge base from Step 2, you now have both structured and unstructured data ready to bring together in a Space.

Step 4: Create a Space

Spaces in Amazon Quick act as unified data workspaces. A Space can hold file uploads, dashboards, knowledge bases, actions, and datasets, giving your chat agent a single location to query across data types.

From the left navigation, select Spaces and create a new Space. Name it “Business Intelligence Hub”.

Add your knowledge base and dataset to the Space:

  1. Choose Add knowledge and select Knowledge bases from the list. Select “Business Knowledge Base” from the list.
  2. Choose Add knowledge again and select Datasets from the list. Select “Product_Sales.csv” from the list.

The Space now shows both your knowledge base (unstructured documents) and your enriched dataset (structured sales data) linked as data sources. This is the central hub where both data types come together, giving your chat agent a single place to query across everything. Figure 7 shows the Space with both resources in the Ready state.

Figure 7: Business Intelligence Hub Space showing the Product_Sales.csv dataset and Business Knowledge Base

Step 5: Create a custom chat agent

Navigate to Chat agents in the left navigation and choose Create chat agent. Amazon Quick presents a prompt builder where you can describe your agent in natural language or choose from templates like Training Guide, Project Coordinator, and Onboarding Helper.

For this walkthrough, choose Skip to configure the agent manually.

Figure 8: Chat agent creation screen with the prompt builder and sample templates

Configure the agent persona

The configuration panel has several sections. Start with the Agent Persona:

  • Agent identity: “Business Intelligence Assistant”
  • Description: “An AI assistant that breaks down information silos by analyzing business data from your knowledge base”

For Agent Persona instructions, enter:

You are a Business Intelligence Assistant designed to help organizations break down information silos. Your primary functions are:

1. Analyze business data stored in S3
2. Retrieve relevant findings from the reports and memos in the knowledge base
3. Provide comprehensive insights that connect internal data with external trends
4. Generate clear, actionable recommendations based on data analysis

When answering questions, always cite your sources and explain how you arrived at your conclusions. Focus on delivering practical business value and highlighting patterns across different information sources.

A note appears confirming that your chat agent comes equipped with enterprise guardrails.

Figure 9: Agent persona configuration with identity and persona instructions filled in

Set communication style

Under Communication style, pick a response style preset. Options include Executive, Technical, and Creative. For a business intelligence use case, select Executive.

Link knowledge sources

Under Knowledge Sources, choose Link spaces and select the “Business Intelligence Hub” Space you created earlier. This gives the agent access to your S3 knowledge base and other data sources in that Space. When you link a Space, the agent answers from large language model (LLM) knowledge and the linked resources only.

You can also attach reference documents (PDF, TXT, HTML, MD, CSV, DOC, DOCX) directly to the agent for additional context. Amazon Quick extracts up to 100,000 characters of text from the reference documents that you upload.

Figure 10: Knowledge Sources section showing the linked Business Intelligence Hub Space

Customize the agent

Under Customization, configure:

  • Welcome message: “Hello! I’m your Business Intelligence Assistant. I can help you analyze your sales data and business documents and provide insights by comparing internal information with market trends. How can I help you today?”
  • Suggested prompts: “Summarize key insights from our reports” and “Analyze our quarterly sales performance”

Figure 11: Customization section with the welcome message and suggested prompts

Launch the agent

Choose Launch chat agent. The right panel shows a live preview of your agent with the welcome message and suggested prompts displayed.

Figure 12: Launched Business Intelligence Assistant with the welcome message and suggested prompts in the chat panel

Step 6: Query across structured and unstructured data

With the agent running, start with a question about your business results:

How did sales change by region in 2025?

For this question, the agent combines results from the Product_Sales.csv dataset with the documents in the S3 knowledge base. It returns a response with regional sales breakdowns, trends, and citations that point back to each source.

Figure 13 shows the response. Each citation marker links a figure back to its source document.

Figure 13: Chat agent response showing regional sales analysis from the dataset and the knowledge base documents

When you ask a question about structured data, the agent uses text-to-SQL to translate your natural language into a SQL query. It runs the query against the dataset and returns the results in a readable format. This means you can ask complex analytical questions without writing SQL yourself.

Next, ask about a specific document:

What are the key strategic priorities outlined in our product strategy memo?

The agent summarizes the strategic pillars, the FY2026 roadmap, and the investment requirements from the Product Strategy Memo, as shown in Figure 14.

Figure 14: Chat agent response summarizing strategic priorities from the Product Strategy Memo

Finally, ask a question that needs both data types:

How do our 2025 sales results align with the market trends identified in our analysis report?

The agent compares the trends in the Market Analysis Report with results from your sales data and cites each source, as shown in Figure 15.

Figure 15: Chat agent response comparing 2025 sales results with market trends from the Market Analysis Report

This is the core value of combining data types in a single Space. The agent can pull from structured CSV data and unstructured documents in the same response. You don’t need to know where the data lives.

Step 7: Generate artifacts and reports using natural language

The Business Intelligence Assistant can also generate formatted documents, including Microsoft PowerPoint presentations, Microsoft Excel spreadsheets, and Microsoft Word documents. Try these prompts in the chat agent:

  • “Create a PowerPoint presentation summarizing AnyCompany’s Q4 2025 sales performance by region, including key trends and recommendations.”
  • “Generate an Excel spreadsheet showing the top 10 orders by revenue with Order ID, Region, Product, and Revenue columns.”
  • “Create a Word document with a quarterly business review summary based on our annual review data.”

Figure 16: Chat agent confirming the request and preparing a PowerPoint outline for AnyCompany’s Q4 2025 sales performance

Figure 17: Generated eight-slide PowerPoint with a downloadable AnyCompany_FY2025_Sales_Performance.pptx file

Step 8: Share the agent

When you launch a chat agent, it remains private until you share it. After you test the agent, share it with your team:

  • From the left navigation, choose Chat agents.
  • In the Actions column for Business Intelligence Assistant, choose the menu icon, and then choose Share.
  • Enter the users or groups to share with, assign Owner or Viewer permissions, and then choose Share.

The agent returns permissions-aware responses, and a knowledge base is available only to its creator until you update its permissions. Make sure that the people you share the agent with also have access to the Space, the knowledge base, and the dataset. For details, see Custom chat agents.

What you accomplished

In this walkthrough, you:

  • Connected Amazon S3 as a data source through an integration.
  • Created a knowledge base that indexes unstructured business documents.
  • Created and enriched a Product Sales dataset for structured data queries.
  • Built a Space that serves as a unified data hub for your chat agent.
  • Configured a custom chat agent with a defined persona and linked knowledge sources.
  • Queried the agent across structured and unstructured data in a single conversation.
  • Generated a PowerPoint presentation from a chat prompt.
  • Shared the agent with your team.

Best practices

Use the following practices as you move from this walkthrough to your own data:

  • Organize your S3 data: Use clear folder structures and file naming conventions. A clear structure also makes it more straightforward to scope a knowledge base to specific S3 prefixes.
  • Write specific persona instructions: The more specific your instructions, the more consistent the agent responses. Include guidance on how to cite sources and handle ambiguous queries.
  • Use Spaces to control scope: Rather than giving an agent access to everything, create focused Spaces with only the data sources relevant to that agent’s purpose.
  • Start with suggested prompts: Suggested prompts help users understand what the agent can do. Choose prompts that demonstrate the agent’s range across both structured and unstructured data.
  • Test before sharing: Use the preview panel to test your agent with representative questions before sharing it with your team.

Security considerations

Under the AWS shared responsibility model, you are responsible for configuring access to your data, knowledge bases, and agents. Consider the following as you adapt this solution:

  • Grant least-privilege S3 access: Give Amazon Quick access only to the buckets that your knowledge bases need. Buckets that an administrator selects have read-only permissions by default. If you create knowledge bases through the API, you can provide a custom AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role for an individual S3 data source instead of granting account-wide S3 access.
  • Control document access: If documents require per-user or per-group access, enable document-level ACLs when you create the knowledge base. You can’t change this choice later.
  • Encrypted buckets: If your bucket uses AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys, follow the AWS KMS steps in the administrator setup guide.
  • Add only trusted content: The agent uses the documents in your knowledge base to form responses, so include only content from sources you trust.
  • Share selectively: Chat agents and knowledge bases are private by default. Share them only with the users and groups that need them.
  • Use guardrails as one layer: Amazon Quick includes built-in content safety screening, and administrators can add up to 50 blocked words or phrases. These controls help reduce risk but don’t replace your responsibility to configure access and permissions. For details, see AI guardrails in Amazon Quick.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, remove the resources you created:

  • Delete the chat agent from the Chat agents page.
  • Delete the Space from the Spaces page.
  • Delete the Product_Sales.csv dataset from the Datasets page.
  • Delete the knowledge base and S3 integration from the Knowledge page.
  • If you created an S3 bucket specifically for this walkthrough, empty and delete it. Deleting a bucket and its objects is permanent, so back up any data that you want to keep.

Amazon Quick user subscriptions and account fees are billed separately from these resources. For details, see Amazon Quick pricing.

Conclusion

Amazon Quick helps you bring structured and unstructured data together. In this post, you connected S3 as a knowledge base, enriched a dataset, built a Space, and created a custom chat agent. Business users can now query both data types through a single conversational interface, without needing to know where the data lives or how to write queries.
