item.title: ServiceNow on-behalf-of token exchange with Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
item.dc:creator: Greg Biegel
item.description: Learn how to configure Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway for an on-behalf-of (OBO) token exchange with Microsoft Entra ID, so an AI agent can call the ServiceNow REST API while preserving the calling user's identity. AgentCore Gateway performs the exchange natively, with no interceptor Lambda or custom code.
item.content:encoded:
AI agents that interact with enterprise APIs on behalf of users need to maintain user identity throughout the request chain. Without identity propagation, API calls arrive at downstream services as the application itself rather than the user who initiated the action. This breaks audit trails, bypasses user-level access controls, and violates the principle of least privilege.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This post shows how to configure AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for an on-behalf-of (OBO) token exchange with Microsoft Entra ID. An AI agent can then call the ServiceNow REST API while preserving the calling user’s identity. You configure the token exchange on the gateway target, and AgentCore Gateway performs the exchange on each request. The pattern can be applied to other REST APIs protected by OAuth.

In production, you can additionally pair identity propagation with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter harmful content and validate the agent’s inputs and outputs.

Solution overview

The architecture involves three key components connected through AgentCore Gateway:

  1. An AI agent application, protected by Microsoft Entra ID through an OAuth application registration.
  2. A Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, implemented using AgentCore Gateway, sitting between the agent and ServiceNow.
  3. The ServiceNow REST API, configured with an inbound OAuth integration tied to Microsoft Entra ID.

The following figure shows the end-to-end solution architecture, including components within AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and ServiceNow.

Figure 1: Solution architecture across AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and ServiceNow

As shown in Figure 1, the user acquires a JSON Web Token (JWT) to invoke the agent 1. The agent authenticates to the gateway with a JWT token scoped to the agent’s own application registration 2. The gateway then exchanges that token, using the OBO flow, for a new token scoped to the ServiceNow API connector, with the original user’s identity preserved 3. ServiceNow receives a valid token whose preferred_username claim maps to an existing ServiceNow user and applies that user’s permissions to the API call 4.

How OBO token exchange works in this context

When the agent calls the gateway, it presents a JWT with an audience claim matching the agent’s client ID (for example, 3ff88e17-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX). ServiceNow, however, expects a token with an audience claim matching its own API connector client ID (5d4a7a11-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX).

The OBO flow bridges this gap. AgentCore Gateway sends the inbound token to the Entra token endpoint along with the agent application’s client credentials, the target scope, and a parameter requested_token_use: on_behalf_of. Entra validates that the calling user consented to the delegation, then issues a new token for the ServiceNow API with the original user’s claims intact.

Prerequisites

Before you begin, you need the following:

  • An AWS account with access to AgentCore Gateway.
  • A Microsoft Entra ID tenant with permissions to create application registrations. Your account needs at least the Application Developer role to register applications.
  • A ServiceNow instance with administrative access to configure inbound OAuth integrations. You can create a ServiceNow personal developer instance (PDI) at the ServiceNow personal developer instance signup page https://developer.servicenow.com/.
  • Two Entra application registrations: one representing the AI agent, and one representing the ServiceNow API connector.

Configuring Microsoft Entra ID

Start by creating an application registration to represent the ServiceNow API connector. The following screenshot shows the application registration page for the ServiceNow API Connector in Microsoft Entra ID.

Figure 2: Application registration for the ServiceNow API connector in Microsoft Entra ID

After creating, in the Overview page note the Application (client) ID.

In the navigation menu expand Manage and select Expose an API and add a scope named user_impersonation using the default Application ID URI. This scope is what the OBO flow requests when exchanging tokens. The following screenshot shows how to expose an API in Microsoft Entra ID.

Figure 3: Exposing the user_impersonation scope in Microsoft Entra ID

Next, create an application registration for the AI agent. The following screenshot shows the application registration page in Microsoft Entra ID for the ServiceNow Agent application.

Figure 4: Application registration for the ServiceNow Agent in Microsoft Entra ID

Note the Application (client) ID for the ServiceNowAgent.

Create a client secret on this registration. The gateway needs these credentials to perform the OBO exchange. The following screenshot shows how you can create a client secret on the ServiceNow Agent application registration in Microsoft Entra ID.

Figure 5: Creating a client secret on the ServiceNow Agent application registration

Then configure the agent application to have API permissions to call the ServiceNow API connector application. The following screenshot shows the API permissions that you need to configure on the ServiceNow Agent application registration in Microsoft Entra ID.

Figure 6: API permission configuration in Microsoft Entra ID

No changes to the Entra configuration are needed beyond what you would set up for any standard OBO integration between two applications.

Configuring ServiceNow

In the ServiceNow administrative console, navigate to System OAuth > Inbound Integrations and create a new inbound integration (Third party ID token issued by OIDC supporting identity provider). Specify the client ID from the ServiceNow API connector application registration you created in Entra. The following screenshot shows the configuration of the inbound integration in ServiceNow.

Figure 7: Configuring the inbound integration in ServiceNow

In the same screen, create a new OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider configuration and enter the OIDC metadata URL for your Entra tenant. Map the user claim to the appropriate user field. For example, if your Entra tenant places the user’s email in the preferred_username claim, map that to the Email field in ServiceNow. Clear JTI verification if your Entra tenant doesn’t include it in tokens. Entra uses an internal claim named uti on tokens it issues, which is equivalent to JTI. Consider mapping this uti claim to a jti claim to provide additional replay protection and denylisting. The following screenshot shows how to configure the OIDC provider in ServiceNow.

Figure 8: Configuring the OAuth OIDC provider in ServiceNow

Finally, in the same screen, create an auth scope for the integration (for example, APIConnector). The following screenshot shows how to create a new auth scope in ServiceNow.

Figure 9: Creating a new auth scope in ServiceNow

Limit the auth scope to the Table API, or whichever ServiceNow APIs your agent needs to access, as shown in the following screenshot.

Figure 10: Limiting the auth scope to the Table API in ServiceNow

After this configuration is complete, ServiceNow accepts authorization tokens with an audience of your API connector’s client ID and resolves the calling user from the preferred_username claim.

Configuring AgentCore Gateway

With Entra and ServiceNow configured, you can now set up AgentCore Gateway to handle the OBO exchange natively.

Step 1: Create an outbound auth configuration

Create a new outbound auth configuration (choose Build > Identity > Add Outbound Auth > Add OAuth client) in AgentCore and select Customized provider. Enter the client ID and client secret from your agent application registration, along with the Entra discovery URL as shown in the following screenshot.

Figure 11: Adding an OAuth client in AgentCore Gateway

Expand Additional configurations and select JWT authorization grant as shown in the following screenshot. This tells the gateway to use a JWT-based grant type for token exchange.

Figure 12: Configuring the JWT authorization grant

Step 2: Create the gateway with MCP version 2025-11-25

Create a new AgentCore Gateway (Build > Gateways > Create gateway). When defining the gateway details, expand Additional configurations — optional and select MCP version 2025-11-25 as shown in the following screenshot. This version is required for native OBO support. You can’t turn on native OBO for gateways created with earlier MCP versions.

Figure 13: Selecting MCP version 2025-11-25

Configure the inbound identity using your agent’s application registration (select Use existing identity provider configurations), as you would for any gateway that accepts Entra-authenticated requests.

Under JWT Authorization Configuration add the Application ID we documented earlier for the ServiceNowAgent as shown in the following screenshot.

Figure 14: Configuring inbound authorization in AgentCore Gateway

Step 3: Add a target with token exchange

Add a target to the gateway pointing to your ServiceNow REST endpoint. Define the schema inline. For example, to expose a tool called ListIncidents that calls the ServiceNow Table API, you can use the following OpenAPI specification (replace the server URL with that for your PDI).

{
  "openapi": "3.0.0",
  "info": {
    "title": "ServiceNow Incident API (Minimal)",
    "description": "A subset of the ServiceNow Table API for listing incident records.",
    "version": "1.0.0"
  },
  "servers": [
    {
      "url": "https://devxxx.service-now.com/api/now/table",
      "variables": {
        "instance": {
          "default": "devxxx",
          "description": "Your ServiceNow instance name."
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "paths": {
    "/incident": {
      "get": {
        "operationId": "getIncidents",
        "summary": "List incidents",
        "description": "Retrieves a list of incident records from the ServiceNow instance.",
        "parameters": [
          {
            "name": "sysparm_limit",
            "in": "query",
            "description": "Maximum number of records to return.",
            "schema": {
              "type": "integer",
              "default": 10
            }
          },
          {
            "name": "sysparm_query",
            "in": "query",
            "description": "An encoded query string to filter results (e.g., active=true).",
            "schema": {
              "type": "string"
            }
          },
          {
            "name": "sysparm_fields",
            "in": "query",
            "description": "A comma-separated list of fields to return.",
            "schema": {
              "type": "string"
            }
          }
        ],
        "responses": {
          "200": {
            "description": "A successful response containing an array of incidents.",
            "content": {
              "application/json": {
                "schema": {
                  "type": "object",
                  "properties": {
                    "result": {
                      "type": "array",
                      "items": {
                        "$ref": "#/components/schemas/Incident"
                      }
                    }
                  }
                }
              }
            }
          },
          "401": {
            "description": "Unauthorized - Invalid credentials."
          }
        },
        "security": [
          {
            "bearerAuth": []
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  },
  "components": {
    "securitySchemes": {
      "bearerAuth": {
        "type": "http",
        "scheme": "bearer",
        "bearerFormat": "JWT"
      }
    },
    "schemas": {
      "Incident": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "sys_id": {
            "type": "string",
            "description": "Unique identifier for the incident."
          },
          "number": {
            "type": "string",
            "description": "Incident ID (e.g., INC0000001)."
          },
          "short_description": {
            "type": "string",
            "description": "A brief summary of the incident."
          },
          "severity": {
            "type": "string",
            "description": "The severity level of the incident."
          },
          "state": {
            "type": "string",
            "description": "The current state of the incident (e.g., New, In Progress, Closed)."
          },
          "sys_created_on": {
            "type": "string",
            "format": "date-time",
            "description": "The timestamp when the incident was created."
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

The following screenshot shows how to configure the REST API target in AgentCore Gateway with the OpenAPI schema.

Figure 15: Configuring the REST API target with the ServiceNow OpenAPI schema

For the Outbound Auth configuration on the target, select OAuth as the outbound identity provider and choose the outbound auth configuration you created in Step 1.

Now expand the Additional configurations section and select Token exchange grant. Configure the following:

Scope: api://5d4a7a11-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx/user_impersonation

This is the scope you exposed on the ServiceNow API connector application registration in Entra.

Custom parameter (key-value pair): requested_token_use:on_behalf_of

This parameter is critical. Without it, Entra doesn’t perform the OBO exchange and the call to ServiceNow fails with an authentication error.

The final configuration is shown in the following screenshot.

Figure 16: Token exchange grant configuration on the AgentCore Gateway target

Step 4: Save and test

Save the target configuration. AgentCore Gateway now automatically exchanges inbound tokens for valid ServiceNow tokens, preserving user identity, with no custom code.

When an agent calls the gateway, the following happens transparently:

  1. The gateway receives the agent’s JWT (audience: agent client ID).
  2. The gateway sends the token to Entra’s token endpoint with the OBO grant type.
  3. Entra issues a new token (audience: ServiceNow API connector client ID) with the original user’s claims.
  4. The gateway forwards the request to ServiceNow with the exchanged token.
  5. ServiceNow resolves the user from the token and applies their permissions.

The following code snippet shows a minimal chat agent that interacts with ServiceNow through the MCP server.

import sys
import strands
from strands.models import BedrockModel
from strands.tools.mcp import MCPClient
from mcp.client.streamable_http import streamablehttp_client

token = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else sys.exit("Usage: python snow_agent.py <TOKEN>")
MCP_URL = "<GATEWAY_URL>"
mcp_client = MCPClient(lambda: streamablehttp_client(url=MCP_URL, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}))
agent = strands.Agent(
    model=BedrockModel(model_id="global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6", streaming=False),
    system_prompt=(
        "You have a tool called 'target-snow___getIncidents'. "
        "When asked about incidents, call it immediately with no parameters. "
        "Never ask the user for credentials or instance details --- the tool is pre-configured."
    ),
    tools=[mcp_client],
)

while (user_input := input("\nYou: ")).lower() not in ("quit", "exit", "q"):
    print(f"\nAgent: {agent(user_input)}")

Troubleshooting

If you receive authentication errors from ServiceNow, verify that:

  • The preferred_username claim in the exchanged token maps to a valid user email in ServiceNow.
  • The auth scope on the ServiceNow inbound integration permits access to the API endpoints your agent is calling.
  • The agent application has API permissions to the ServiceNow API connector application in Entra.

Cleaning up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the following resources if you created them for testing:

  • The AgentCore Gateway and its targets.
  • The outbound auth configuration.
  • The Entra application registrations (if created specifically for this walkthrough).
  • The ServiceNow inbound integration and OIDC provider configuration.

Conclusion

The native OBO support in AgentCore Gateway removes the need for custom AWS Lambda interceptors to perform token exchanges. You configure the token exchange directly on the gateway target, and the gateway handles it transparently on every request. This approach maintains user identity across the agent-to-API chain, supports ServiceNow’s user-level access controls, and eliminates custom code that would need to be maintained separately.

To get started with AgentCore Gateway, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation. For more on Microsoft Entra’s OBO flow, refer to the Microsoft identity platform documentation.

item.title: How Gen Digital built Norton Revamp’s AI-curated News Engine with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search
item.dc:creator: Iskander Sanchez-Rola
item.description: Gen Digital built Norton Revamp, a generative AI-powered professional reputation management platform, with an AI-curated News Engine grounded by Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. See how the Gen team delivers real-time, cited content suggestions, goal setting, and news feeds with zero data egress and Norton-grade privacy.
item.content:encoded:
Your professional reputation now lives online first. Recruiters check LinkedIn before returning a call. Clients review your digital presence before booking a first meeting. For ambitious professionals, that shift is an opportunity: a well-crafted online voice can open doors that a résumé alone never could.

But standing out takes more than content generation. It takes real-time awareness of what’s happening right now. A professional building a reputation as a generative AI thought leader needs to react to today’s breakthroughs, not last week’s headlines. And with feeds flooded by AI-generated noise, audiences reward authenticity and timeliness more than ever.

Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore made that possible. We built Norton Revamp, a generative AI-powered professional reputation management platform. At its heart is an AI-curated News Engine, powered by AgentCore Web Search, that grounds every content suggestion, goal recommendation, and news feed item in current, cited web knowledge. The platform launched in March 2026, built by a small group of engineers.

In this post, we show you how the Gen team builds an AI-curated News Engine in Norton Revamp with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search to help customers turn ideas into engaging social media posts.

The challenge: Real-time grounding for professional content

Unlike chatbots that rely on static knowledge bases, Norton Revamp needs to understand what’s trending right now in each user’s professional domain. A cyber security expert needs today’s threat intelligence. A marketing leader needs this week’s industry shifts. Traditional approaches (custom web crawlers, third-party news APIs, static content databases) each carry trade-offs: infrastructure overhead, stale data, vendor complexity, or data egress risk.

We evaluated three alternatives before choosing AgentCore Web Search. Custom crawlers require ongoing maintenance and lag real time. Third-party news APIs added vendor contracts, API key management, and data leaving our AWS environment. Static knowledge bases were perpetually stale. AgentCore Web Search eliminated these concerns. It’s fully managed with zero infrastructure overhead, operates entirely within AWS with zero data egress, and returns cited sources with URLs and publication dates. This makes personalized, real-time news feeds viable at scale.

How AgentCore Web Search powers Norton Revamp

Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a fully managed web search capability, compliant with the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It’s available as a managed connector on the AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Our agent sends a natural-language query, and Web Search returns relevant snippets, source URLs, titles, and publication dates that the model uses to produce grounded responses.

This capability powers three core features:

AI-curated news feed

Every user gets a personalized content stream surfacing the latest articles and trending topics tied to their goal. If you’re building a reputation as a generative AI thought leader, your feed prioritizes AI breakthroughs, industry analysis, and emerging use cases, sourced in real time through AgentCore Web Search. Unlike a static RSS aggregator, the feed is a goal-aware discovery engine that refreshes with every session.

Smart content suggestions

Users receive AI-generated content ideas tailored to trending topics in their space, written in their own authentic voice, with optional AI-generated visuals. AgentCore Web Search grounds every suggestion on what’s happening today. A three-step coaching flow (Analyze, Refine, Post) walks users from initial ideas to published content on LinkedIn and X, with a feedback loop, so the AI gets sharper with every iteration.

Trend-aware goal setting

Users define a goal. The AI builds a personalized roadmap with weekly themes and milestones. AgentCore Web Search feeds real-time trend data into goal generation, so weekly themes reflect current industry movements. The system learns from the past four weeks of activity, refreshing recommendations as users grow.

Architecture and tech stack

Figure 1: Event-driven architecture of the Norton Revamp News Engine

The integration follows an event-driven architecture. When a user sets or updates their professional goal, Amazon Nova (through Amazon Bedrock) generates targeted search queries based on the goal, recent activity, and engagement patterns. The agent sends these queries to AgentCore Web Search, which returns cited results entirely within our AWS environment. Our AI Learning System ranks the results for relevance, recency, and source credibility. The ranked results then serve as grounding context for Amazon Nova Lite to generate content suggestions in the user’s authentic voice. Engagement data feeds back into query generation, making the News Engine progressively smarter.

Generative AI and machine learning stack:

  1. Amazon Bedrock – Core generative AI engine for content generation, personalization, post analysis (batch mode), and content coaching.
  2. Amazon Nova (Nova Lite) – Primary large language model (LLM) powering content generation, goal creation, and trend analysis.
  3. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Real-time web retrieval powering the News Engine, content grounding, and trend discovery through an MCP-compliant managed connector.
  4. Stability AI – Image generation.
  5. Claude (through Amazon Bedrock) – Additional LLM capabilities for complex reasoning tasks.

Infrastructure: React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS on the frontend. Node.js, Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB (multi-table with composite key patterns), Amazon API Gateway, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), Amazon EventBridge, Amazon CloudFront, Amazon CloudWatch, and AWS Secrets Manager on the backend. Infrastructure managed through Terraform with blue-green deployment for zero-downtime releases.

Processing pipeline: The platform runs four pipeline stages:

  1. Full Scan – Pull up to 1,000 historical posts, store in Amazon S3, run Amazon Bedrock batch analysis for reputation impact.
  2. Daily Scan – Amazon EventBridge-triggered incremental analysis.
  3. Weekly Goal Generation – Lambda generates goals considering past engagement data plus real-time trend data from AgentCore Web Search.
  4. Content Coaching – Synchronous Amazon Bedrock calls through the Analyze, Refine, Post flow, each step grounded with AgentCore Web Search results.

Engineering with an AI-native development mindset

We embedded generative AI from day one, as both the product and the development methodology. The human-AI responsibility split was deliberate: human-owned architecture decisions, security reviews, business logic, and personalization algorithms. AI handled code generation, documentation, test scaffolding, refactoring, and UI component creation.

With Claude, we produced 10 or more design variants per concept, compressed design-to-prototype time from weeks to hours and generated 70 percent of UI code with AI. We tested five pricing models in the time previously needed for one. The gamification system went through eight iterations before launching.

The measurable impact: 3x faster feature implementation, boilerplate generation accelerated by 90 percent, documentation by 80 percent, test creation by 70 percent, and UI component generation by 65 percent. The trade-off: AI output review consumed 20–30 percent of our time.

AI helped with personalization algorithms, the DynamoDB multi-table architecture (which needed experience-based judgment), security implementation, and Amazon Bedrock batch processing optimization. The key insight: AI accelerated implementation, but humans designed how the AI Learning System should adapt to user goals. Product generative AI (Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Nova, AgentCore Web Search) and development generative AI served different purposes, and we kept them separate.

Testing, security, and quality assurance

We achieved 85 percent code coverage through automated test generation. Critical test areas included content generation quality, AgentCore Web Search result relevance and freshness validation, engagement tracking accuracy, gamification logic, and news feed relevance to user goals.

For a product carrying the Norton brand, compliance is non-negotiable. Security checks spanned static code analysis, dependency vulnerability scanning, authentication flows, user data encryption, access control logic, generative AI model output validation, and content filtering. Our security team reviewed all AI-generated recommendations: AI accelerated identification, and humans made final decisions.

The result: 99.9 percent uptime since launch with real-time monitoring of generative AI content quality and user satisfaction.

Best practices for AgentCore Web Search integration

For teams considering AgentCore Web Search for real-time grounding:

  1. Invest in query generation – Well-structured queries yield better results than open-ended ones, so we focused on our prompt engineering there.
  2. Cache strategically – Real-time freshness is the point, but some queries don’t need to re-execute every session. We cache results with time-to-live (TTL) values that match freshness requirements.
  3. Build feedback loops – Track which web search results users engage with and feed that signal back into query generation. Our News Engine’s relevance improved over the first 90 days.
  4. Validate source quality – AgentCore Web Search returns source URLs and publication dates. We built a lightweight credibility scoring layer to prioritize authoritative sources.

Conclusion

Building Norton Revamp proved that a small, generative AI-augmented team can deliver enterprise software in months. It also proved that Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore can serve as the real-time intelligence backbone for products that need to stay current with the world.

We launched a generative AI-native professional reputation management platform in months, with personalized goal setting, AI-driven content suggestions, real-time curated news feeds grounded by AgentCore Web Search, adaptive learning, gamification, and Norton-grade security. A small group of engineers achieved 99.9 percent uptime.

Generative AI doesn’t replace engineers. It amplifies them. Pairing that amplification with fully managed services like AgentCore Web Search removes entire categories of infrastructure complexity. Humans designed the vision. Generative AI through Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Nova, and AgentCore Web Search accelerated bringing it to life, grounded in real-time, cited web knowledge.

“Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore eliminates the complexity of building and maintaining our own web retrieval infrastructure. It lets our Norton Revamp News Engine deliver real-time, personalized content grounded in what’s happening in each user’s professional domain, with zero data egress and Norton-grade privacy. We went from concept to production in months, and AgentCore Web Search was a key enabler.”

To learn more about Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, visit the AgentCore documentation. Check out Norton Revamp.

item.title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI with EDB Postgres AI and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.dc:creator: Rajesh Nagpal
item.description: Learn how to build a governed semantic layer for agentic AI inside EDB Postgres AI and query it from a Strands Agents agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Business meaning, join paths, and access control all live in Postgres, with GRANT and row-level security enforcing what each agent can read.
item.content:encoded:
In this post, we show how to build a semantic layer for agentic AI using EDB Postgres AI. We run a Strands Agents agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that queries the layer to answer customer 360 (C360) questions. Earlier posts in this series built the same C360 pattern with Stardog’s knowledge graph, Denodo’s data virtualization platform, AtScale’s dimensional model, and Strategy Mosaic’s linked models.

EDB Postgres AI puts the semantic layer inside the operational Postgres database as an AIDB extension. Business meaning lives next to the data in standard Postgres COMMENT statements, the join graph comes from Postgres foreign keys, and governance uses Postgres GRANT and row-level security through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that ships with AIDB.

By the end of this post you will know:

  • How to build an AIDB semantic knowledge base (SemKB) over a Postgres schema, how COMMENT ON statements and aidb.create_semantic_alias behave as the authoring surface, and how foreign keys crawl into join paths.
  • How to expose the AIDB tool catalog to an external agent through the built-in EDB MCP endpoint, fronted by an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and registered as an MCP target on AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
  • How Postgres roles, column-level GRANT statements, and row-level security produce different results for different callers. The prompt, tool catalog, and agent code stay the same.
  • How AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces for every SQL execution as rows in the aidb_otel schema, queryable with ordinary SQL.

Three layers an agent needs

An agent that answers business questions from live data needs three layers: a model that plans and writes queries, a meaning layer that tells the agent what the data represents, and a runtime that hosts the agent and controls identity and access. The Stardog post in this series introduced this framing. The model layer in this post is Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock, the same as prior posts (model availability varies by AWS Region). The runtime layer is AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore Gateway handles inbound authorization, and AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, holds outbound credentials for the tool targets, same as prior posts. EDB Postgres AI hosts agents and tools inside the database itself and acts as the connection point for external agents through its MCP endpoint.

The meaning layer is where this post diverges from the others. Here it is a SemKB that lives inside the operational Postgres database. The schema and the business definitions are indexed together. Postgres GRANT, row-level security, and column-level grants enforce access, not an advisory system prompt. The sections that follow cover how AIDB builds the layer, how AgentCore exposes it, and how two Postgres roles asking the same question get different answers.

Example use case: C360 on EDB Postgres AI

The dataset is the Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit, loaded into a single EDB Postgres AI instance in a dedicated c360 schema. The data model has four tables and one derived view.

Object Key columns
customers cid, first_name, last_name, full_name, email, ssn, phone, picture, location (FK to locations.id)
locations id, city, state, zip
products id, name, brand, dept, price
purchases id, cid (FK to customers.cid), pid (FK to products.id), date, quantity, price
big_spender (view) cid, full_name, state, large_orders, largest_order

The physical schema is a plain Postgres join graph: a customer in the customers table lives at a location, places purchases, and each purchase references a product. The semantic work rests on three business ideas that column names don’t reveal.

State isn’t on the customer row. It lives in locations, reached through the customers.location foreign key, and a comment on that column tells SemKB where to find it.

purchases.price records the order total. An agent that reads it as a unit price and multiplies by quantity returns $502,529 for the top customer instead of $27,991.66.

Big spender is a term the business owns. Captured as a view with a COMMENT ON VIEW statement, its definition stays in one place that every agent, dashboard, and query reads from.

The questions we run through the agent end to end:

  1. Who are our top 10 customers by total spend, and what state is each in?
  2. How many big spenders do we have in each state?
  3. Can you list 10 customers and the state each lives in?
  4. Which 10 products have sold the most units?
  5. Can you list five customers with their Social Security numbers? (used in the governance rerun).

Reference architecture

The following diagram shows the request path from the analyst through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to the semantic layer inside EDB Postgres AI. The analyst authenticates with Amazon Cognito and calls AgentCore Gateway with the issued JSON Web Token (JWT) as a Bearer token. Gateway routes to AgentCore runtime, which plans with Claude on Amazon Bedrock. The agent calls MCP tools through Gateway, which forwards to an Application Load Balancer in the EDB Postgres AI virtual private cloud (VPC) and on to the edb-endpoints MCP server inside AIDB. AIDB serves the SemKB, semantic aliases, and read-only PostgreSQL tables. AgentCore traces go to Amazon CloudWatch, and AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces as rows in the aidb_otel schema inside Postgres.

Figure 1: Reference architecture for EDB Postgres AI and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Two flows cross the boundary between AgentCore and EDB Postgres AI.

Inbound: A client calls AgentCore Gateway with a bearer token issued by an Amazon Cognito user pool. The Gateway inbound JWT authorizer validates the token against the Cognito discovery URL. Gateway then evaluates its Cedar policy against the token’s claims to decide which tools this agent, acting for this user, can invoke. It then routes the call to AgentCore runtime. The agent invokes Claude on Amazon Bedrock for planning and answer composition.

Outbound to the semantic layer: The agent’s tool call is an MCP request. AgentCore Gateway supports MCP server targets directly. AIDB’s edb-endpoints HTTP server speaks streamable HTTP MCP with HTTP Basic authentication, which lets Gateway treat it as an MCP server target with no translation layer. An Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener and an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate fronts edb-endpoints on an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance. The ALB URL is registered as the Gateway target. The AgentCore Identity credential provider holds the Postgres role credential and injects it as Basic auth on every outbound request. The agent code doesn’t see the Postgres credential.

Observability: AgentCore emits traces for tool calls, large language model (LLM) calls, and token usage to CloudWatch Transaction Search. AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces for SQL execution as rows in the aidb_otel schema inside Postgres, queryable with ordinary SQL after the database is configured to write them (see enabling telemetry on the source database).

No AWS Lambda is required in this architecture. AIDB already speaks MCP, so Gateway talks to it as an MCP server target directly through the ALB. The Denodo post in this series uses the same ALB pattern in front of its MCP server, and the architecture here is unchanged other than the vendor.

Build the semantic layer

These steps assume AIDB is installed and enabled on the EDB Postgres AI instance and the Stardog C360 kit’s four CSVs are loaded into a dedicated c360 schema with the primary and foreign keys shown earlier. Because this layer lives in the same database as the data, there is no second system to deploy and no catalog to synchronize. The semantic layer is defined in SQL, inside the same database as the application that writes the rows.

An AIDB semantic knowledge base indexes Postgres schema, not data. It embeds the definition of every table, view, and column (with the COMMENT ON text alongside) into a vector store that an agent can search in natural language. Three authoring tasks help the agent find the right table and column by meaning: writing COMMENT ON statements, defining business terms as views with their own comments, and registering recurring questions as semantic aliases. Comments are the simplest of the three authoring tasks and improve text-to-SQL accuracy the most for both users and agents.

Add comments where the agent will look

COMMENT ON COLUMN c360.purchases.price IS
  'Total amount the customer paid for the entire order, in US dollars. Not the unit price.';
COMMENT ON COLUMN c360.purchases.cid IS
  'Customer who placed the order. Joins to customers.cid.';
COMMENT ON COLUMN c360.customers.location IS
  'Home address of the customer. Joins to locations.id. State is in locations.state.';
COMMENT ON COLUMN c360.customers.ssn IS
  'US Social Security number. Sensitive, column-level grant required.';

CREATE VIEW c360.big_spender AS
  SELECT c.cid, c.full_name, l.state,
         count(*)      AS large_orders,
         max(pu.price) AS largest_order
    FROM c360.purchases pu
    JOIN c360.customers c ON c.cid = pu.cid
    JOIN c360.locations l ON l.id  = c.location
   WHERE pu.price > 250
   GROUP BY c.cid, c.full_name, l.state;

COMMENT ON VIEW c360.big_spender IS
  'Big spenders. A big spender is a customer with at least one order over 250 US dollars. '
  'Use this view for any question about big spenders.';

The view holds the business definition in one place, so no agent or dashboard has to redefine big spender. The time you spend on comments up front pays off on every query the agent runs afterward.

Create the semantic knowledge base

Create the SemKB over the c360 schema. The call registers the name, the embedding model, the target schemas, and the auto-processing mode.

SELECT aidb.create_semantic_kb(
    name            => 'c360_kb',
    model           => 'bge-small-en-v1.5-f16',
    schemas         => ARRAY['c360'],
    auto_processing => 'Live'
);

The embedding model is a local llama.cpp model (llamacpp_embeddings) that ships with the AIDB Amazon Machine Image (AMI). SemKB uses one embedding model per KB, so every entry sits in the same vector space. The AIDB AMI ships with a default SemKB named semkb over public, so creating c360_kb leaves two SemKBs on the instance. When more than one SemKB exists, every aidb.semantic_kb_search call must pass kb_name explicitly. To swap the local model for a remote embedding model, such as Amazon Titan Text Embeddings on Amazon Bedrock, register the remote model with aidb.create_model. Pass its name as the SemKB’s model parameter. The auto_processing parameter accepts Disabled, Live, or Background. Live reacts to schema changes through Postgres event triggers. Background processes them asynchronously from a worker. Disabled waits for an explicit aidb.refresh_semantic_kb(). SemKB also crawls foreign keys into relationships at the same time. The purchases.cid foreign key becomes a join path the agent can discover by meaning, not by column name.

Capture recurring questions as semantic aliases

A semantic alias is a named, parameterized read-only SELECT with a natural-language description that SemKB indexes alongside the schema metadata. The agent finds it by meaning, calls it with parameters, and returns a governed answer.

SELECT aidb.create_semantic_alias(
    name        => 'big_spenders_by_state',
    description => 'Count big spenders grouped by state, ordered from most to fewest.',
    query_text  => $$SELECT state, count(*) AS big_spenders
                     FROM c360.big_spender
                     GROUP BY state
                     ORDER BY big_spenders DESC, state$$,
    params      => '[]'
);

Aliases are AIDB’s reusable text-to-SQL building block. They sit next to tables and views in the SemKB index and show up to an agent as a tool. For a full text-to-SQL walkthrough, see the EDB documentation.

Govern access

Governance in this architecture runs through Postgres primitives all the way down. The AIDB MCP endpoint has no permission system of its own: “Postgres grants decide what each agent can run” (MCP endpoint reference). Each MCP request authenticates with a Postgres username and password over its own connection, so current_user inside every tool call is the agent’s role, visible in pg_stat_activity like other connections.

The following diagram traces how identity flows from the end user through AgentCore to the Postgres role that evaluates the SQL, and how the resulting trace is captured for audit. The chain runs in four phases: inbound trust at the Gateway, outbound credential from AgentCore Identity, enforcement in Postgres through GRANT and row-level security, and audit through OpenTelemetry traces in the aidb_otel schema.

Figure 2: Identity propagation chain from the end user to the Postgres role that evaluates the SQL

Inbound trust at Gateway: 1. The end user authenticates with Amazon Cognito and receives a JWT bearer token. 2. The client calls AgentCore Gateway with the token in the Authorization header. 3. The Gateway JWT authorizer validates the token against the Cognito user pool’s discovery URL. 4. Gateway evaluates its Cedar policy against the token’s claims to decide which tool this agent can call.

Outbound credential to AIDB: 5. Gateway resolves the outbound credential for the MCP target from the AgentCore Identity credential provider. For AIDB, this is a Postgres username and password used as HTTP Basic auth. 6. Gateway forwards the MCP streamable-HTTP request to the ALB, which forwards it to edb-endpoints.

Enforcement in Postgres: 7. edb-endpoints opens a Postgres connection using the username and password from the Basic auth header. Postgres authenticates the login role per pg_hba.conf, and current_user inside the tool call is that role. 8. Column-level GRANT statements and row-level security policies on c360 tables enforce what rows and columns the tool call returns. A denial surfaces as a Postgres permission-denied error on the restricted table or column, which the MCP endpoint forwards unchanged.

Audit. 9. AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces for the SQL execution as rows in the aidb_otel schema, available through SQL immediately.

Two Postgres roles, same question, different results

Define two agent login roles that differ only in a column-level GRANT: mcp_agent_full sees every column, mcp_agent_restricted sees every column except customers.ssn.

CREATE ROLE mcp_agent_full       LOGIN PASSWORD '...';
CREATE ROLE mcp_agent_restricted LOGIN PASSWORD '...';

GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA c360 TO mcp_agent_full, mcp_agent_restricted;

-- Both roles need aidb_users to list MCP tools
GRANT aidb_users TO mcp_agent_full, mcp_agent_restricted;

-- Full role sees every column
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA c360 TO mcp_agent_full;

-- Restricted role sees every table and view, with customers.ssn withheld
GRANT SELECT ON c360.locations, c360.products, c360.purchases, c360.big_spender
  TO mcp_agent_restricted;
GRANT SELECT (cid, first_name, last_name, email, phone, picture, location, full_name)
  ON c360.customers TO mcp_agent_restricted;

Both login roles need password-auth entries in pg_hba.conf for the local edb-endpoints connection path, as covered in configuring your agent role. Running the same question through both roles produces different results. The agent calling under mcp_agent_restricted can’t project the ssn column: the moment it tries, Postgres returns permission denied for column ssn and the MCP endpoint forwards that error unchanged. The agent then responds that it can’t read SSNs. The prompt, the tool catalog, the SemKB, and the agent code are identical between the two roles. The only difference is the credential AgentCore Identity injects on the outbound Basic auth header.

Row-level filtering follows the same pattern. Enable row-level security (RLS) on a target table and attach per-role USING policies. The AIDB MCP endpoint sees the same rows the role would see in a direct psql connection.

A note on AIDB purposes. AIDB also ships purposes, a policy abstraction that confines in-database agents (those created with aidb.create_agent and invoked with aidb.agent_converse) to a named Postgres role. Purposes apply to the in-database agent path. The external AgentCore path this post uses governs through Postgres roles directly at the MCP endpoint, as described earlier. For audit of external MCP agents, see EDB Agent Governance, which reads the same aidb_otel spans and visualizes agent sessions and policy decisions.

Responsible AI considerations. The governance surface shown so far controls what the agent can execute at the database layer. Pair it with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails on the model side to shape what the agent is allowed to generate: content filters for sensitive topics, denied-topic lists, and PII redaction. The two layers complement each other. Postgres GRANT stops the agent from reading SSNs at the data layer. Guardrails help prevent PII patterns from leaking through other paths in the model response. For agents answering business questions over customer data, both are production controls.

Expose the layer and run the agent

Enabling the AIDB MCP endpoint takes two Postgres parameters plus a restart. Set edb.endpoints_mcp_enabled = on in postgresql.conf, add aidb to shared_preload_libraries, and restart (enabling the endpoint). To reach the endpoint from outside the EC2 instance, set edb.endpoints_mcp_host to a non-loopback address such as 0.0.0.0. Choose a port with edb.endpoints_mcp_port (default is 8765). Supply the Transport Layer Security (TLS) pair with edb.endpoints_mcp_tls_cert and edb.endpoints_mcp_tls_key, which the endpoint requires for non-loopback binds (configuring the endpoint).

An Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener and an ACM certificate exposes edb-endpoints to AgentCore Gateway. The ALB target group uses HTTPS to the EC2 instance on port 8765 and doesn’t validate the backend certificate chain, so a self-signed certificate on edb-endpoints is sufficient for development and testing. For production, use an internal ALB with AgentCore Gateway VPC egress to keep connectivity between Gateway and the ALB private.

Create an AgentCore Gateway with a Cognito authorizer, register the ALB URL as an MCP server target, and store the two Postgres credentials in the AgentCore Identity credential provider (credential provider reference).

The agent is a short Python script. It uses Strands Agents to wire a BedrockModel pointing at the latest Claude Sonnet to an MCPClient. The MCPClient connects to the Gateway URL over the streamable HTTP MCP transport with the Cognito access token as a Bearer header. The system prompt instructs the agent to call semantic_kb_search first for schema context, passing kb_name => 'c360_kb', then execute_sql to run the generated query. The AgentCore runtime starter toolkit with Strands has a worked example of hosting an agent of this shape in production.

We recommend turning on Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the agent’s system prompt. The same instruction and the same tool list are reused on every call, which is what prompt caching is for.

Sample queries and verification

Four questions through the agent plus one governance rerun, all against the C360 data loaded earlier.

Query 1: Who are our top 10 customers by total spend, and what state is each in?

Without the comment on purchases.price, an agent configured with only a SQL execution tool reads price as a unit price and multiplies by quantity. The top row comes back as roughly $502,529 for Carolyn Inworth, which is wrong. One column comment, indexed by SemKB, is the entire difference between that answer and the right one:

     full_name     |     state      |   spent
-------------------+----------------+----------
 Carolyn Inworth   | Wisconsin      | 27991.66
 Marlane Shadwick  | Florida        | 22677.05
 Isaac Popping     | Pennsylvania   | 20085.96
 Bria McKellar     | Texas          | 19588.80
 Mike Laydel       | Louisiana      | 18651.28
 Fayette Mor       | Arizona        | 17993.69
 Reynard Perigoe   | Florida        | 17019.55
 Humfrey Fores     | California     | 16811.16
 Patrice Jakeway   | California     | 16656.72
 Mord Pettus       | North Carolina | 16604.37

Same model, same prompt, same tool catalog. The semantic knowledge base changes the answer.

Query 2: How many big spenders do we have in each state?

The agent finds the big_spender view through semantic_kb_search because its COMMENT ON VIEW matches the natural-language question. The business definition sits in exactly one place:

        state         | big_spenders
----------------------+--------------
 Florida              |           46
 Texas                |           46
 California           |           42
 District of Columbia |           24
 New York             |           23
 ...

If the business later redefines a big spender as a customer with cumulative spend over $5,000, the change is one CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW statement. Every agent sees the new definition the next time SemKB refreshes.

Query 3: List 10 customers and the state each lives in

The state is in locations, not customers. The join path is encoded in the customers.location foreign key and in the column comment, both indexed by SemKB. The agent emits:

SELECT c.cid, c.full_name, l.state
  FROM c360.customers c
  JOIN c360.locations l ON l.id = c.location
 ORDER BY c.cid
 LIMIT 10;
 cid |       full_name       |     state
-----+-----------------------+----------------
   1 | Jolynn Bithany        | Texas
   2 | Mord Pettus           | North Carolina
   3 | Lavinie Stannislawski | Florida
   4 | Kimball Evenett       | Alabama
   5 | Linnie Meatcher       | California
   6 | Lorens Stoneley       | Washington
   7 | Juliane Gerhartz      | California
   8 | Jacob O'Lyhane        | Utah
   9 | Terrel Seller         | Missouri
  10 | Jannel Gawthrope      | California

Query 4: Which 10 products have sold the most units?

A plain aggregation that runs inside Postgres next to the data:

SELECT p.name, sum(pu.quantity) AS units
  FROM c360.purchases pu
  JOIN c360.products  p  ON p.id = pu.pid
 GROUP BY p.id, p.name
 ORDER BY units DESC, p.id
 LIMIT 10;
        name        | units
--------------------+-------
 Markers            |   160
 Cleaning Wipes     |   155
 Playset (Girl's)   |   146
 Queen Sheet Set    |   138
 Mechanical Pencils |   137
 Shot Glasses       |   133
 Parchment Paper    |   127
 American Cheese    |   127
 Pop Music          |   127
 Varnish            |   125

Governance rerun: List five customers with their Social Security numbers

The same prompt runs twice. Under mcp_agent_full, the agent returns five customer rows with their ssn values populated. Under mcp_agent_restricted, the agent’s tool call fails with the Postgres error permission denied for column ssn, and the agent responds with a short message that SSNs are not accessible to this caller. The failure is enforced by the column-level GRANT, not by the prompt or the model. AIDB captures the OpenTelemetry trace for the SQL execution in aidb_otel, so a reviewer can query the trace row to confirm the governance decision later.

Extending across data sources

For analytical workloads that outgrow the operational database, EDB Postgres Analytics Accelerator (PGAA) lets Postgres read Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Parquet tables in object storage through an Iceberg REST catalog. The EDB Postgres AI analytics overview covers the end-to-end setup. PGAA tables appear in Postgres as ordinary tables, so the same SemKB description keeps working against the analytical copy and the agent’s tool catalog doesn’t change.

For federation to external relational sources, Postgres foreign data wrappers make an external table reachable as if it were local. The semantic layer is unchanged in either case because business definitions, column comments, and semantic aliases live in Postgres.

Deployment

Two shapes work for this architecture.

Self-managed on Amazon EC2. Use the EDB Postgres AI Agent Factory AMI from the AWS Marketplace. The customer owns the VPC, the subnet, the version cadence, and the EDB Postgres AI software upgrades. The ALB and the AgentCore Gateway target configuration are unchanged from the preceding architecture.

EDB-managed on Amazon EC2. EDB Managed Database is a service where EDB experts handle database administration on the customer’s behalf. The AgentCore side is unchanged.

Conclusion

Reliable agentic analytics needs three things working together: a foundation model that can plan and generate queries, a semantic layer that provides a governed business view of the data, and an agent runtime that hosts the agent and manages identity. Amazon Bedrock supplies the model, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore supplies the runtime, and EDB Postgres AI supplies a semantic layer that lives inside the operational Postgres database. Business meaning, join paths, and governance come from Postgres primitives already present in the schema. The AWS side is the same as the rest of this series: AgentCore Gateway, Runtime, Identity, Bedrock, and CloudWatch.

The data, the business definitions, and the access rules all live in one Postgres schema, so there is no separate catalog to keep in sync. Audit lives in the same database: aidb_otel holds a span per tool call, next to the data it ran against.

Where to start

To apply this architecture to your own data, work through these steps:

  1. Pick one Postgres database your agents need to query live. Narrower is better.
  2. Create a dedicated schema for the agent’s data, with GRANT USAGE scoped to a service role.
  3. Write COMMENT ON statements on columns and views that use business language. Capture business terms as views with a COMMENT ON VIEW statement.
  4. Create a SemKB over the schema with aidb.create_semantic_kb and auto_processing => 'Live' (or Background under high write volume).
  5. Register recurring questions as semantic aliases.
  6. Enable the AIDB MCP endpoint, front it with an ALB with HTTPS and an ACM certificate, and register the ALB URL as an AgentCore Gateway MCP server target.
  7. Run three real questions through the agent, then rerun one under a role with reduced grants to confirm the enforcement surface works end to end.

item.title: Building ultra-low-latency voice AI applications on AWS
item.dc:creator: Nolan Chen
item.description: Learn how Cartesia, an AWS Partner, uses purpose-built State Space Models and AWS infrastructure to deliver sub-100ms text-to-speech and speech-to-text at global scale, and how to deploy its Sonic model on Amazon SageMaker AI or self-managed Amazon EC2 GPU instances.
item.content:encoded:
Conversational AI is transforming how humans interact with technology. From virtual assistants and AI-powered contact centers to real-time translation and accessibility tools, voice-first interfaces are rapidly becoming the default mode of interaction for millions of users worldwide.

Yet delivering a truly natural voice experience remains one of the hardest challenges in AI infrastructure. Users expect human-like responsiveness. Excess latency can break conversational flow and erode trust. To feel natural, AI-generated speech must arrive within the same temporal window as human turn-taking.

This post introduces how Cartesia, an AWS Partner specializing in real-time voice AI, uses purpose-built State Space Models (SSMs) and AWS infrastructure to deliver sub-100ms text-to-speech and speech-to-text at global scale. Developers can build voice experiences that feel indistinguishable from human conversation.

The rise of conversational AI and latency expectations

The demand for real-time voice AI is growing rapidly across industries:

  • Contact centers: AI agents handling millions of customer interactions require instantaneous speech generation to maintain natural dialogue.
  • Telehealth: Remote patient consultations demand low-latency voice for accurate, empathetic communication.
  • Gaming and virtual worlds: Immersive experiences require real-time voice synthesis for non-player characters (NPCs) and player interactions.
  • Accessibility: Screen readers and voice interfaces must respond instantly to serve users with visual impairments.
  • Inbound and outbound sales: AI sales agents must respond without awkward pauses to qualify leads, handle objections, and keep prospects on the line.

Traditional transformer-based text-to-speech (TTS) models struggle with streaming latency because they process entire sequences before producing output. This architectural limitation creates a fundamental tension: higher quality often means higher latency. A new class of models, State Space Models, resolves this trade-off.

AI for voice: State Space Models (SSM)

State Space Models (SSMs) take a fundamentally different approach to processing sequences than transformers, the architecture behind most of today’s AI. Transformers use a mechanism called attention, which compares every element in a sequence to every other element. As a result, the amount of computation grows quadratically as the sequence gets longer. SSMs instead treat a sequence as a system that evolves continuously over time, processing it step by step and carrying a compact internal state forward. This can be converted into a form computers handle efficiently, keeping the cost low for certain long sequences. This efficiency makes SSMs well suited to real-time, streaming data like live speech.

Key advantages of SSMs for audio processing include:

  • High-quality long-range dependencies: Structured SSMs are a form of linear recurrence, but their state parameterization preserves information over long audio sequences, avoiding the long-range signal decay that limits classic recurrent neural networks (RNNs) such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks.
  • Constant memory footprint: Unlike transformers that cache all previous tokens, SSMs maintain a fixed-size hidden state.
  • Native streaming support: The recurrent structure processes input token-by-token, so it supports true streaming without architectural modifications.

These properties make SSMs uniquely suited for real-time voice applications where both quality and latency are non-negotiable.

How it works: SSMs for real-time voice

Cartesia puts these SSM advantages to work in two production voice models: Sonic for speech generation and Ink for transcription.

Introducing Cartesia

Cartesia is a real-time multimodal intelligence company that has built a voice AI application, purpose-built on State Space Model architecture. Founded by researchers who pioneered SSM advances, Cartesia’s application is designed for streaming inference at the edge of human perception.

The application features two core models, Sonic for text-to-speech and Ink for speech-to-text, both optimized for sub-100ms first-byte latency while maintaining studio-quality output.

Sonic (text-to-speech)

Sonic is Cartesia’s flagship streaming text-to-speech model, delivering ultra-realistic speech synthesis with sub-100ms latency:

  • First audio byte in approximately 90ms: Users hear the voice respond almost instantaneously.
  • Ultra-realistic voice quality: Natural prosody, emotion, and expressiveness across over 44 languages.
  • Voice cloning with minimal data: Create natural-sounding custom voices from 10-second audio samples.
  • Streaming-native architecture: Audio begins generating before the full text input is received.
  • Context-aware synthesis: Maintains consistent tone and style across long passages.

Sonic is recommended for teams that want the fastest time-to-production with minimal operational overhead. Call the API and receive streaming audio in real time.

Ink (speech-to-text)

Ink is Cartesia’s streaming speech-to-text model, purpose-built for conversational AI applications:

  • Native turn detection: Automatically identifies when a speaker has finished their turn, alleviating awkward pauses without a separate voice activity detection (VAD) or end pointing model.
  • Context-aware end pointing: Uses semantic understanding to distinguish between mid-sentence pauses and true conversation boundaries.
  • Streaming transcription: Emits partial transcripts in real time as the user speaks, so a downstream large language model (LLM) can begin forming its response before the turn ends.
  • Noise robustness: Maintains accuracy in noisy environments common in real-world deployments.
  • Multi-speaker support: Handles overlapping speech and speaker transitions gracefully.

Together, Sonic and Ink provide the complete voice AI stack needed to build conversational agents that feel human.

Deploying Cartesia on AWS

If you need data sovereignty, latency control, or compliance, you can deploy Cartesia models directly into your own AWS account. Sonic is delivered as an Amazon SageMaker AI model package through AWS Marketplace, which you deploy to a SageMaker AI endpoint running entirely within your virtual private cloud (VPC). Inference data doesn’t leave your account.

The deployment patterns in this section cover Sonic. Ink is currently available through the Cartesia API, which you can purchase through the Cartesia Voice AI Platform listing in AWS Marketplace. Two primary patterns are available for Sonic.

Option 1: Amazon SageMaker AI (AWS Marketplace model package)

Deploying on Amazon SageMaker AI is the fastest path to a managed, in-VPC Sonic endpoint. Sonic ships as an AWS Marketplace model package, so there’s a one-time subscribe step that grants your account an AWS Region-specific model-package ARN. You then create the SageMaker AI endpoint from that ARN, either from the console or with the SageMaker or Boto3 SDK. The following steps follow Cartesia’s official deployment notebook.

Prerequisites

Run from an Amazon SageMaker Notebook Instance or SageMaker Studio.

The AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role needs AmazonSageMakerFullAccess.

To subscribe, your role (and you) need aws-marketplace:Subscribe, aws-marketplace:Unsubscribe, and aws-marketplace:ViewSubscriptions. Otherwise, the account must already be subscribed to the listing.

Before deployment, choose a supported instance type from the model package’s SupportedRealtimeInferenceInstanceTypes field:

  • ml.g6e.xlarge or larger
  • ml.g7e.2xlarge or larger
  • ml.g7.2xlarge or larger
  • ml.p5.48xlarge
  • ml.p5en.48xlarge

If your chosen instance type’s applied value is below your current usage plus your planned endpoint instance count, you may need to request a service quota increase. See SageMaker AI quotas for details.

Deploy Sonic 3.6 to a SageMaker endpoint

In Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, you can subscribe to its AWS Marketplace model package, create a SageMaker model, and host it on a real-time endpoint. The following four steps show the deployment path.

  1. In SageMaker AI, open AWS Marketplace resources, then All products. Search for Sonic 3.6 SageMaker and choose the Cartesia listing.

    Figure 1: Searching AWS Marketplace for the Cartesia Sonic 3.6 SageMaker model package

  2. Choose View purchase options, review the pricing and terms, and subscribe. The subscription grants your AWS account access to the model package. It doesn’t deploy resources.

    Figure 2: The Cartesia Sonic 3.6 listing in AWS Marketplace

  3. Open Deployments & inference > Deployable models, choose Create model, select Use a model package subscription from AWS Marketplace, and select Sonic 3.6 SageMaker. Choose an execution role, then create the model.

    Figure 3: Creating a SageMaker model from the Sonic 3.6 subscription

  4. Create a real-time endpoint from the model with a supported GPU instance, such as ml.g6e.2xlarge. The endpoint first appears with Creating status. Wait for InService before invoking it.

    Figure 4: The SageMaker endpoint for Sonic 3.6

The model-package ARN is Region-specific. To verify the Sonic 3.6 package in US East (N. Virginia) with the SageMaker API, run:

export MODEL_PACKAGE_ARN="arn:aws:sagemaker:us-east-1:865070037744:model-package/sonic36-sagemaker-v0-c6e9cacffcdf31178d1bd7c98c587480"

aws sagemaker describe-model-package \
    --model-package-name "$MODEL_PACKAGE_ARN" \
    --region us-east-1 \
    --query '{Status:ModelPackageStatus,ProductId:InferenceSpecification.Containers[0].ProductId,InstanceTypes:InferenceSpecification.SupportedRealtimeInferenceInstanceTypes}'

After the endpoint reaches InService, invoke it with the SageMaker Runtime InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream API and process the returned audio stream in your application.

Option 2: Self-managed on EC2 GPU instances

Some teams have existing GPU infrastructure, strict networking requirements, or a need to co-locate Cartesia with other services. For these cases, you can run the model container yourself on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) GPU instances. This gives you full control over the runtime, scaling, and network path. It uses Cartesia’s container image, obtained from Cartesia, rather than the AWS Marketplace model package.

Figure 5: Self-managed deployment flow for Cartesia Sonic on Amazon EC2 GPU instances

Obtain the container image. Request the Sonic container image and licensing terms from Cartesia. Replicate it into your own private Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository so your compute plane can pull it with IAM-scoped credentials rather than reaching out to an external registry at scale.

Choose your GPU instance family. Sonic runs on NVIDIA GPU instances. The G6 (L4) and G6e (L40S) families are the optimal balance for real-time TTS. The earlier G5 (A10G) also works. Match GPU memory and vCPU to your target concurrency and prefer a single-GPU instance per model replica for simplest scaling.

Provision the compute plane (Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS)). For ECS: register a GPU task definition (set the container’s GPU resource requirement, for example, resourceRequirements with type GPU) and run it as a service behind an Application Load Balancer. For EKS: create a GPU node group (or Karpenter provisioner) using the EKS GPU-optimized AMI, install the NVIDIA device plugin, and deploy the container as a Deployment fronted by a Service/Ingress.

Configure networking for low latency. Place inference nodes in a cluster placement group to minimize inter-node latency, keep replicas in a single Availability Zone for the tightest path, and use VPC endpoints for ECR/S3 pulls. For hybrid or on-premises callers, terminate traffic over AWS Direct Connect or a private Network Load Balancer to avoid public-internet hops.

Load model weights efficiently. Store model weights on a shared, low-latency volume (Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) or Amazon FSx for Lustre) mounted across replicas so new pods/tasks start without each re-downloading multi-GB artifacts. Warm the model at container start and expose a health check so the load balancer only routes to ready replicas.

Tune batching and concurrency. Set the container’s max batch size and concurrent-stream limits to match your traffic profile. Higher batch size improves GPU utilization but adds first-byte latency, so tune against your sub-100ms target. Benchmark streams-per-GPU to find the replica capacity you will scale on.

Implement custom auto scaling. Scale on a signal that reflects real load, active audio-stream count or GPU utilization, rather than CPU. On Amazon ECS, use AWS Application Auto Scaling with a custom Amazon CloudWatch metric. On Amazon EKS, use HPA/KEDA driven by a GPU or stream-count metric, with Karpenter (or Cluster Autoscaler) adding GPU nodes as replicas grow.

Add observability and resiliency. Emit latency (time-to-first-byte), stream counts, and GPU metrics to CloudWatch. Run at least two replicas across nodes for availability. Set rolling-update or draining policies so deployments don’t drop in-flight audio streams.

This approach is recommended when integrating Cartesia into an existing machine learning (ML) system, meeting networking or compliance requirements not available through managed services, or optimizing cost with Reserved or Spot GPU capacity. The trade-off is that you own provisioning, scaling, patching, and monitoring that SageMaker would otherwise handle for you.

Learn more: See Amazon ECS task definitions for GPU workloads, managing NVIDIA GPU devices on Amazon EKS, and getting started with GPU-accelerated EC2 instances.

Choosing the right deployment pattern

AWS offers two ways to run Sonic, each suited to a different starting point.

The managed path, using the Amazon SageMaker AI model package from AWS Marketplace, is the default for most teams: you subscribe, deploy to an in-VPC endpoint in minutes, and let SageMaker handle scaling and operations.

The self-managed path, running the model container yourself on EC2 GPU instances, is designed for teams with specific constraints: existing GPU infrastructure, strict networking requirements, or a need to co-locate Cartesia with other services. For these teams, full control over the runtime, scaling, and network path matters more than time to deployment.

The following table summarizes how the two compare.

Criteria SageMaker (Marketplace) EC2 GPU (Self-Managed)
Time to Deployment Minutes after subscribing Hours to days
Compute Real-time endpoint. See SupportedRealtimeInferenceInstanceTypes for supported instances. EC2 GPU instances
Operational Control Managed by AWS Full control
Scaling SageMaker automatic scaling Custom scaling policies
Cost Model Software fee + per instance hour + infra EC2 (Reserved/Spot savings)
Networking In-VPC endpoint (network isolation) Placement groups, Direct Connect
Best For Fast, managed, in-VPC Custom infra, max control

Beyond deploying Cartesia in your own account, these models are already proven in production inside Amazon services, and few environments are more demanding for real-time voice than a live contact center. Amazon Connect is exactly that proving ground.

In production: Amazon Connect

This section shows how Cartesia’s voice models operate inside Amazon Connect at production scale.

What is Amazon Connect?

Amazon Connect is a cloud-based contact center service that businesses use to set up and run customer support operations that handle inbound and outbound voice calls, chat, and messaging. With pay-as-you-go pricing and deep integration with AWS services, Amazon Connect powers millions of customer interactions daily across industries from financial services to healthcare.

How Cartesia powers the Amazon Connect experience

Cartesia’s voice AI models integrate natively with Amazon Connect to deliver next-generation contact center experiences:

  • Instant responsiveness: Alleviate unnatural pauses that erode customer confidence in AI-powered interactions.
  • Real-time transcription: Ink provides live transcription with intelligent turn detection for agent-assist workflows.
  • Multilingual support: Serve customers in over 44 languages with consistent voice quality and natural prosody.
  • Scalable infrastructure: Handle traffic spikes during peak hours without degradation in voice quality or latency.

By combining the omnichannel orchestration of Amazon Connect with Cartesia’s real-time voice AI, you can automate complex customer interactions while maintaining the natural, responsive experience that builds trust and loyalty.

Getting started

Ready to build ultra-low-latency voice AI applications? Here are next steps:

  • Deploy Sonic through SageMaker JumpStart: Search for “Cartesia” in the SageMaker JumpStart model hub and deploy a real-time endpoint in minutes.
  • Try the Cartesia API: Get started with the Cartesia get-started guide. No infrastructure setup required.
  • Explore reference architectures: Visit the Cartesia GitHub repository for sample notebooks, deployment templates, and integration examples.
  • Contact the team: Reach out to Cartesia on AWS Marketplace.
